harder.updated_question: preventing hallucinations in abstractive summarization models by improving training data
harder.verification_criterion: The answer identifies at least one specific method for improving training data quality or composition that has been shown to reduce hallucinations in abstractive summarization models.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to preventing hallucinations in abstractive summarization by improving training data, with concrete techniques and measured trade-offs.

# What “hallucination” means in summarization and why it happens
Hallucinations in abstractive summarization are claims in the summary that are unfaithful to the source document—either intrinsic (verbatim copying from the source) or extrinsic (generated content not present in the source) and often erroneous even when plausible.<cite id="7240312b-1">Intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations happen frequently—more than 70% of single-sentence summaries contain hallucinations, and over 90% of extrinsic hallucinations are erroneous</cite><cite id="7240312b-2">NLU-driven pretraining helps but does not solve hallucination; ROUGE/BERTScore are insufficient and semantic-inference metrics better reflect faithfulness and factuality</cite>.<cite id="7240312b-0">Benchmarks like XSum hallucination annotations, FRANK, and related resources were created to probe factuality and enable detection/evaluation of hallucinations in abstractive outputs</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-2">Extrinsic hallucinations can be accurate if the model has external world knowledge, but empirical analyses show models are primarily inaccurate on extrinsic hallucinations</cite>.

A large source of errors is training data quality: summarizers trained on noisy or conflicting signals produce more hallucinations, and the degree of hallucination correlates with data quality.<cite id="66e8e430-0">The degree of a model's hallucinations correlates with training data quality; models trained on XSum produce more factual errors than CNN/DM</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Noisy data are common in public datasets; removing noisy samples reduces hallucinations but shrinks data and diversity, hurting ROUGE and information recall</cite>.

# How to improve training data to reduce hallucinations

## 1) Curate and clean: filter noisy, conflicting, and hallucinatory examples
Training on cleaner data directly reduces hallucination rates. But indiscriminate filtering can hurt recall and diversity, so curricula that preserve task-relevant knowledge are preferred.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Removing noisy XSum samples (e.g., entity-precision filtering retaining 24.6% of data) reduces hallucinations but drops ROUGE by 8–18% and entity recall by 20%, illustrating the recall-diversity trade-off</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-1">A practical remedy is to train “clean” and “noisy” experts and combine their parameter differences to adjust a base model (CaPE), reducing hallucinations without significant ROUGE or information recall loss</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Use factuality/faithfulness annotations (e.g., XSum hallucination labels, FactCC) to stratify data and down-weight or reweigh conflicting, hallucinatory examples.<cite id="7240312b-0">XSum provides human annotations for faithfulness and factuality on 500 texts; FRANK aggregates 2,250 summaries with factuality annotations to benchmark models</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-2">FactCC provides expert-annotated validation/test splits and a synthetic portion for training inconsistency detectors</cite>.
- Apply automated, scalable verifiers as weak labels (e.g., entity-level entailment or posterior probabilities) to triage large corpora before training.<cite id="3e837f81-0">Entity-level classifiers using masked language model priors/posteriors detect hallucinated entities and improve factuality when used as rewards</cite>.

## 2) Train with verifiable references and citations
Requiring explicit attribution to source spans reduces unfaithful content and makes summaries user-verifiable. Synthetic data pipelines can bootstrap such training when labels are scarce.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Citation-grounded summarization forces models to attribute claims to source text; we propose synthetic data generation with automated verification to train grounded models, yielding an 84% LLM-as-judge accuracy vs. 43–56% for baselines while supporting very long documents</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Prior work leverages citations to construct summaries (cluster/score citation-linked sentences), though relying solely on citations may omit context; combining citations with citation-context mitigates this</cite><cite id="66e8e430-4">Citation-context and citation-network-aware methods capture contributions and link citing/ cited sentences; LLMs enhance feature extraction and pairing for citation-based summarization</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Augment training with labeled or synthetically verified claim→supporting-span pairs; constrain decoding to only summarize information supported by cited spans.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Synthetic teacher-generated data with automated verification enables training citation-grounded models at scale</cite>.
- Prefer datasets with rich structural signals (e.g., scientific discourse, citation graphs) to learn when and how to cite for verifiability.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Citations help select central claims, but must be complemented with context to avoid omitting circumstances and assumptions</cite>.

## 3) Reduce copying hallucinations via architecture and training signals
Pointer/coverage mechanisms curb extractiveness but can still over-copy long spans; structured representations and explicit selection improve abstractiveness and faithfulness.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Pointer-generator mixes copy and generate distributions and introduces a coverage loss to penalize repeated attention, reducing repetition and improving ROUGE</cite><cite id="c310bff1-2">Coverage maintains a cumulative attention vector to avoid revisiting the same source words, discouraging repetition</cite><cite id="c310bff1-3">Despite enabling abstraction, pointer-generator models often copy whole sentences; StructSum reduces copied-sequence length by 9.13 words on average and increases novel n-grams by 14.7% while matching task performance</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Add explicit content-selection layers or structured encodings (e.g., discourse/argument structure) and train with selection masks so the generator must justify content it introduces.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Bottom-up pipelines first select relevant source spans (sequence tagging) then summarize over masked relevant content</cite>.
- Use coverage regularization and copy-penalties during training; add token-level hallucination detection losses to discourage unsupported copying.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Coverage loss effectively eliminates repetition and improves ROUGE</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-3">Token-level detection of hallucinations can be done “for free” during generation, enabling joint summarization and self-check with minimal overhead</cite>.

## 4) Learn from factuality signals: entity-level rewards and attribute/claim supervision
Entity-level and attribute-level supervision targets a major driver of hallucinations—spurious new entities or claims not grounded in evidence.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Approximately 30% of entities in state-of-the-art summaries are hallucinated; over half of these hallucinated entities are factual (document/world knowledge), so entity-level supervision can substantially improve factuality</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">An automatic Entity Hallucination Index (EHI) focuses on named-entity faithfulness and can serve as a scalable reward for RL fine-tuning, promoting entity-grounded summarization without additional human labels</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Train with entity/attribute-level reward models (EHI, masked LM-based posterior priors) and use RL or reward-weighted sampling to favor faithful entity usage.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level reward signals improve factuality classification and hallucination detection, and improve summarization factuality when used for guidance</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-1">EHI-based reward fine-tuning promotes entity-grounded summarization without extra supervision, outperforming coarse factuality rewards</cite>.
- Incorporate NLI-based inconsistency detection to flag claims conflicting with source facts and use it to reweight training losses or constrain hypothesis space.<cite id="3e837f8a-2">NLI-based inconsistency detectors (e.g., Polytope categories; SUMMAC Conv trained on FactCC-derived data) label inconsistent summaries and can be trained on synthetic inconsistencies</cite>.

## 5) Use faithfulness-aware objectives and evaluation to guide data-centric improvements
Training without faithfulness signals can improve ROUGE while increasing hallucinations; thus, optimize for semantic-level faithfulness and measure both automatic and human metrics.<cite id="7240312b-2">Pretraining improves faithfulness but remains far from solving hallucination; ROUGE/BERTScore are insufficient—semantic inference metrics better capture true quality</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Pretraining improves faithfulness on future data but can also hallucinate outdated information based on parametric knowledge, demonstrating trade-offs between temporal generalization and veracity</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Co-train with factuality rewards (EHI, entity posterior priors) and faithfulness objectives (semantic inference/QuestEval/FEQA-like signals) to reduce hallucinations without harming coverage or ROUGE too much.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">Entity-level rewards reduce entity hallucinations and can be integrated directly into training</cite>.
- Evaluate with FRANK, FactCC, and domain-specific hallucination suites to ensure reductions generalize beyond ROUGE.<cite id="7240312b-0">FRANK benchmarks factuality across models by generating and annotating summaries, complementing XSum hallucination resources</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-2">FactCC provides expert-labeled splits and synthetic data for training/evaluating inconsistency detection</cite>.

## 6) Curriculum and domain adaptation: select, then summarize
Training with explicit selection of relevant content reduces hallucinations by constraining the generator to source subsets and improving abstractiveness and faithfulness.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Content selection (sequence tagging) chooses relevant source tokens and masks irrelevant parts, preventing the model from copying extraneous content</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-3">CNN/DailyMail exhibits fewer training-time hallucinations than XSum; token-level detection combined with repurposed factuality datasets improves precision-recall trade-offs for hallucination detection</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Pre-train selection modules to identify key spans and train summarizers with span-masks that enforce summarization over selected content only.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Bottom-up summarization: select relevant tokens first, then summarize under the mask</cite>.
- For scientific/citation-rich domains, train with citation-context discourse models that learn when to cite and how much context to include for faithful verification.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Citations alone may omit context; combining citation content with discourse structure better reflects the original paper’s evidence and assumptions</cite>.

# What to expect: measured effects and trade-offs
- Direct reductions in hallucination prevalence and improved factuality metrics: entity-level filtering and rewards reduce hallucinated entities and factuality errors, including on XSum and related datasets.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level supervision reduces hallucinated entities and improves overall factuality when used as a reward</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-1">Entity-Hallucination Index-based RL fine-tuning promotes entity-grounded summarization</cite>.
- Improved abstractiveness and reduced extractive copying: structured representations and content-selection reduce long-copy spans and increase novel n-grams while preserving quality.<cite id="c310bff1-3">StructSum reduces copied sequence length by 9.13 words and increases novel trigrams by 21% vs. pointer-generator, matching task performance</cite>.
- Trade-offs with recall and ROUGE: aggressive filtering and purely extractive biases can hurt coverage and scores; balanced curricula and hybrid objectives mitigate these losses.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Entity-precision filtering (XSum→24.6% data) reduces hallucinations but drops ROUGE 8–18% and entity recall 20%, stressing the need for curriculum that preserves task knowledge</cite><cite id="66e8e430-1">CaPE leverages both clean and noisy data and reduces hallucinations without significant ROUGE or recall drops</cite>.
- Long-term reliability and verifiability: citation-grounded training with synthetic verification yields higher adjudicated accuracy and enables auditing for very long documents.<cite id="66e8e430-2">A 24B grounded model achieves 84% LLM-as-judge accuracy vs. 43–56% for open-weight baselines and can summarize texts up to 2M tokens with reliable attribution</cite>.

# Practical checklist for data-centric hallucination mitigation
- Audit your training corpus: stratify by faithfulness/factuality labels; identify noisy/conflicting examples; apply entity-level verifiers as weak labels.<cite id="7240312b-0">Human-annotated hallucination resources (XSum, FRANK) and FactCC enable targeted filtering and benchmarking</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level classifiers using masked LM posteriors improve detection and can guide data triage</cite>.
- Add verifiable references: include span-level citations in training and constrain decoding to cited content; synthesize with automated verifiers when ground truth is scarce.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Synthetic data with automated verification trains citation-grounded models; explicit attribution enables user verification</cite>.
- Teach the model what to copy and when not to: train content selection layers and coverage penalties; prefer pointer/coverage variants and structured representations to curb long-copy spans.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Coverage loss reduces repetition; bottom-up selection masks irrelevant content</cite><cite id="c310bff1-3">Structured encodings reduce sentence-level copying and increase novel n-grams</cite>.
- Optimize with faithfulness rewards: integrate entity/attribute-level rewards (EHI, posterior priors) into the loss or RL curriculum; evaluate with FRANK/FactCC and semantic-inference metrics.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">EHI provides a scalable, entity-focused reward to reduce hallucinations</cite><cite id="7240312b-2">Semantic-inference metrics better capture faithfulness than ROUGE</cite>.
- Balance quality: monitor information recall, ROUGE, and novelty; use contrastive ensembling or curriculum mixing of clean/noisy data to retain diversity while reducing hallucinations.<cite id="66e8e430-1">Contrastive parameter ensembling leverages clean and noisy samples to reduce hallucinations with limited ROUGE/recall degradation</cite>.

# Summary
Improving training data—by curating and cleaning noisy examples, adding verifiable citations and entity/attribute-level supervision, constraining models to summarize only selected, supported content, and optimizing with faithfulness-aware rewards—consistently reduces hallucinations in abstractive summarization across datasets and domains.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Hallucination severity correlates with training data quality, and targeted filtering reduces errors though it risks recall loss</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level supervision addresses a large share of hallucinated entities and improves overall factuality</cite><cite id="66e8e430-2">Citation-grounded training with synthetic verification yields high adjudicated accuracy and verifiable outputs at scale</cite><cite id="c310bff1-3">Structured, selection-driven models reduce extractive copying while maintaining quality</cite>. The most robust systems combine data triage with reference/citation grounding and faithfulness-aware training objectives, evaluated with factuality benchmarks rather than ROUGE alone.<cite id="7240312b-2">ROUGE/BERTScore are insufficient for faithfulness; semantic inference metrics align better with human judgments</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-1">Entity-level rewards provide scalable supervision for faithful summarization</cite>.

Snippet: To date, various resources (e.g., datasets/benchmarks) have been made available for studying hallucination detection. Title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We conducted a large-scale study of hallucinations in abstractive document summarization. Title: Towards Attribute-Entangled Controllable Text Generation: A Pilot Study of Blessing Generation
Snippet: Hallucinations in abstractive summarization are model generations that are unfaithful to the source document. Current methods for detecting hallucinations operate mostly on noun phrases and named entities, and restrict themselves to the XSum dataset, which is known to have hallucinations in 3 out of 4 training examples (Maynez et al., 2020). We instead consider the CNN/DailyMail dataset where the summarization model has not seen abnormally many hallucinations during training. We automatically detect candidate hallucinations at the token level, irrespective of its part of speech. Our detection comes essentially for free, as we only use information the model already produces during generation of the summary. This enables practitioners to jointly generate a summary and identify possible hallucinations, with minimal overhead. We repurpose an existing factuality dataset and create our own token-level annotations. The evaluation on these two datasets shows that our model achieves better precision-recall tradeoffs than its competitors, which additionally require a model forward pass.
</snippet>

Title: Reducing Hallucinations in Summarization via Reinforcement Learning with Entity Hallucination Index
Snippet: Hallucination in Summarization. Hallucination, or the generation of content that is unfaithful to the input, is a long-standing challenge in abstractive summarization (Maynez et al., 2020). Several studies have quantified hallucination prevalence across datasets and models (Pagnoni et al., 2021). Techniques such as constrained decoding (Cao et al., 2020) and fact-checking-based reranking (Goyal et al., 2022) have been proposed to mitigate hallucination during or after generation. 

Entity-Level Hallucination Detection. Prior work has recognized the importance of entity-level evaluation for factuality. Metrics like FEQA (Durmus et al., 2020) and QuestEval (Scialom et al., 2021) attempt to assess factual consistency using question answering techniques. However, these methods often require reference summaries or external QA systems, limiting scalability. Our work builds on this line by employing the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI), a lightweight evaluation metric focusing specifically on named entity faithfulness. 

Reward-Driven Fine-Tuning. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has gained traction for aligning model outputs with desired qualities, such as factuality and helpfulness (Ouyang et al., 2022). In summarization, factualityaware reward models have been used for finetuning (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018). Unlike previous approaches that rely on coarse factuality rewards or human-labeled datasets, we propose finetuning using EHI as a direct, automatic reward signal, thereby promoting entity-grounded summarization without additional supervision.
</snippet>

Title: SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization
Snippet: (eXtreme Summarization Faithfulness, XSF) (Maynez et al., 2020) is a dataset with models trained on the XSum dataset (Narayan et al., 2018) which consists of more abstractive summaries than CoGenSumm. The authors find that standard generators remain consistent for only 20-30% of generated summaries. The authors differentiate between extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations (which we call inconsistencies in this work). Extrinsic hallucinations, which involve words or concepts not in the original document can nonetheless be accurate or inaccurate. In order for a summarizer to generate an accurate extrinsic hallucination, the summarizer must possess external world knowledge. Because the authors found that the models are primarily inaccurate in terms of extrinsic hallucinations, we map both extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations to a common inconsistent label. 

Polytope (Huang et al., 2020) introduces a more extensive typology of summarization errors, based on the Multi-dimensional Quality Metric (Mariana, 2014). Each summary is annotated with eight possible errors, as well as a severity level for the error. We standardize this dataset by labeling a summary as inconsistent if it was annotated with any of the five accuracy errors (and disregarded the three fluency errors). Each summary in Polytope was labeled by a single annotator, making it impossible to measure inter-annotator agreement. 

FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020) contains validation and test splits that are entirely annotated by authors of the paper, because attempts at crowdsourced annotation yielded low inter-annotator agreement. Prior work (Gillick and Liu, 2010) shows that there can be divergence in annotations between experts and non-experts in summarization, and because the authors of the pa-per are NLP researchers familiar with the limitations of automatic summarizations, we expect that FactCC annotations differs in quality from other datasets. FactCC also introduces a synthetic dataset by modifying consistent summaries with semantically variant rules. We use a sub-portion of this synthetic dataset to train the SUMMAC Conv model.
</snippet>

Title: Automatic Evaluation of Attribution by Large Language Models
Snippet: Summarization involves condensing a given passage or article into brief sentences while preserving its original meaning. To simulate contradictory examples, we use datasets with annotations of hallucinations. In terms of XSum-Hallucination (Maynez et al., 2020), we merge examples with the same ID and consider those with the most intrinsic hallucination as contradictory and those with the most extrinsic hallucination as extrapolatory. Paired full articles and ground truth summaries are treated as attributable examples. For XENT (Cao et al., 2022), 'Non-factual Hallucination' and 'Intrinsic Hallucination' are seen as contradictory, 'Factual Hallucination' as extrapolatory, and 'Non-hallucinated' as attributable. Each article and reference are paired as attributable examples. Finally, we resplit the manually annotated dev and test sets for training and evaluation in FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020), with 'INCORRECT' labeled as extrapolatory and 'CORRECT' as attributable.
</snippet>

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Neural abstractive summarization systems have been shown to generate plausible summaries with high lexical overlap with the references. However, human analyses (Fabbri et al., 2021a;Pagnoni et al., 2021;Tejaswin et al., 2021) and automatic evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2020;Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020) show that state-of-the-art models trained on the widely used XSUM (Narayan et al., 2018) and CNN/DM (Hermann et al., 2015)   information with high frequency. The degree of a model's hallucinations further correlates with the quality of the training data (Aralikatte et al., 2021;Pagnoni et al., 2021). For instance, models trained on the XSum data tend to generate a higher proportion of factual errors as compared to models trained on the CNN/DM dataset. 

Given the association between training data quality and hallucinations in resulting models, the easiest method to reduce hallucinations is to remove noisy samples from the training data (Nan et al., 2021). However, data filtering reduces the size of training data and consequently, the diversity in target summary since the removed noisy samples might also include useful task-specific knowledge. This impacts other aspects of the generated summaries such as information recall or fluency. In Table 1, we show ROUGE (R-1/2/L) and named entity recall (E-R ref ) with respect to the reference summary of a BART model (Lewis et al., 2020) trained on the entity precision-filtered XSUM data (24.6% of the original data). The new model drops 8-18% in ROUGE and 20% drop in entity recall. 

In this work, we design a simple yet effective strategy to utilize both clean and noisy training samples.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We present Contrastive Parameter Ensembling (CaPE) to reduce content hallucinations in abstractive summarization models. We first select clean (noisy) training samples to fine-tune an expert (antiexpert) model. Then, we use the difference between the parameters of expert and anti-expert models to adjust the parameters of a base summarization model. We evaluate CaPE on the XSUM and CNN/DM datasets using a diverse set of factual metrics, finding that CaPE effectively reduces hallucinations without a significant drop in ROUGE and information recall.
</snippet>

Title: sui-1: Grounded and Verifiable Long-Form Summarization
Snippet: Large language models excel at summarization but frequently generate unfaithful content, including fabricated facts or misattributed claims that users cannot trust without laboriously verifying against source documents. Citation-grounded summarization addresses this by requiring models to explicitly attribute claims to source text, enabling users to quickly assess reliability and trace claims to their origins. 

Training citation-grounded models presents challenges: standard datasets lack citation annotations, manual annotation is prohibitively expensive, and the task requires precise coordination between content generation and source reference. We address these challenges through synthetic data generation using a capable teacher model, with automated verification ensuring citation accuracy before training. 

We introduce sui-1, a 24B parameter model achieving 84% overall accuracy on LLM-as-a-judge evaluation compared to 43-56% for baselines (Figure 1). The model notably outperforms all tested open-weight baselines, demonstrating that task-specific training provides greater benefit than scale alone. sui-1 reliably processes documents exceeding 100 pages, with iterative chunking enabling summarization of texts up to 2 million tokens.
</snippet>

Title: Scientific Article Summarization Using Citation-Context and Article’s Discourse Structure
Snippet: Training the discourse parser requires large amount of training data in the RST framework. 

Scientific article summarization was first studied by Teufel and Moens (2002) in which they trained a supervised Naive Bayes classifier to select informative content for the summary. Later Elkiss et al. (2008) argue the benefits of citations to scientific work analysis. Cohan et al. (2015) use a search oriented approach for finding relevant parts of the reference paper to citations. Qazvinian and Radev (2008;Qazvinian et al. (2013) use citations to an article to construct its summary. More specifically, they perform hierarchical agglomerative clustering on citations to maximize purity and select most central sentences from each cluster for the final summary. Our work is closest to Qazvinian and Radev (2008) with the difference that they only make use of citations. While citations are useful for summarization, relying solely on them might not accurately capture the original context of the referenced paper. That is, the generated summary lacks the appropriate evidence to reflect the content of the original paper, such as circumstances, data and assumptions under which certain findings were obtained. We address this shortcoming by leveraging the citation-context and the inherent discourse model in the scientific articles.
</snippet>

Title: When Large Language Models Meet Citation: A Survey
Snippet: Aggregating all citation sentences referring to a paper can yield a significant amount of information about the paper itself (Abu-Jbara and Radev, 2011). Citation-based summarization harnesses the citations from a scientific article or its reference citation network to assemble a succinct summary. The summary aims to highlight the main contributions of papers, based on citation sentences from papers that cite the source document. The initial attempt uses sentence clustering and ranking methods (Luo et al., 2023). 

With the progression of research, automatic citation-based summarization can be broadly divided into two distinct categories as follows: (a) document-level citation context span based summarization (Qazvinian and Radev, 2008). Techniques involving span identification and varied feature extraction have been utilized (Cohan and Goharian, 2015); (b) citation network structured aware summarization. More recent research works put forward the idea that citation graphs can be instrumental in creating top-notch summaries of scientific papers (Chen et al., 2022;Luo et al., 2023). LLMs, with their proficiency in deriving complex text representations from dense vectors and generating high-quality text, are gaining prominence in complex tasks like citation-based summarization. Hence, there's an enhanced capability to encode citation context and integrate citation network graphs, thereby further boosting citation-based summarization efforts (Luo et al., 2023). Document-level Features. Given their superior capability to derive text representation from textual input, LLMs can be employed for capturing document-level features within a citation recommendation system. Saini et al. (2023) introduce a multi-view clustering approach that utilizes dualembedding spaces and citation contexts for document summarization, leveraging document encoders like BERT, GPT-2, and XLNET to capture document-level features. Roy and Mercer (2022) propose a method for establishing connections between citing sentences and corresponding citation sentences in the referred literature. Their framework pairs every sentence in a publication with all sentences from the referenced document, then seeks to identify semantically similar pairs. The selected sentences from the referenced paper, which have semantic similarities with the publication's sentences, are considered cited statements.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to preventing hallucinations in abstractive summarization by improving training data, with concrete techniques and measured trade-offs.

# What “hallucination” means in summarization and why it happens
Hallucinations in abstractive summarization are claims in the summary that are unfaithful to the source document—either intrinsic (verbatim copying from the source) or extrinsic (generated content not present in the source) and often erroneous even when plausible.<cite id="7240312b-1">Intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations happen frequently—more than 70% of single-sentence summaries contain hallucinations, and over 90% of extrinsic hallucinations are erroneous</cite><cite id="7240312b-2">NLU-driven pretraining helps but does not solve hallucination; ROUGE/BERTScore are insufficient and semantic-inference metrics better reflect faithfulness and factuality</cite>.<cite id="7240312b-0">Benchmarks like XSum hallucination annotations, FRANK, and related resources were created to probe factuality and enable detection/evaluation of hallucinations in abstractive outputs</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-2">Extrinsic hallucinations can be accurate if the model has external world knowledge, but empirical analyses show models are primarily inaccurate on extrinsic hallucinations</cite>.

A large source of errors is training data quality: summarizers trained on noisy or conflicting signals produce more hallucinations, and the degree of hallucination correlates with data quality.<cite id="66e8e430-0">The degree of a model's hallucinations correlates with training data quality; models trained on XSum produce more factual errors than CNN/DM</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Noisy data are common in public datasets; removing noisy samples reduces hallucinations but shrinks data and diversity, hurting ROUGE and information recall</cite>.

# How to improve training data to reduce hallucinations

## 1) Curate and clean: filter noisy, conflicting, and hallucinatory examples
Training on cleaner data directly reduces hallucination rates. But indiscriminate filtering can hurt recall and diversity, so curricula that preserve task-relevant knowledge are preferred.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Removing noisy XSum samples (e.g., entity-precision filtering retaining 24.6% of data) reduces hallucinations but drops ROUGE by 8–18% and entity recall by 20%, illustrating the recall-diversity trade-off</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-1">A practical remedy is to train “clean” and “noisy” experts and combine their parameter differences to adjust a base model (CaPE), reducing hallucinations without significant ROUGE or information recall loss</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Use factuality/faithfulness annotations (e.g., XSum hallucination labels, FactCC) to stratify data and down-weight or reweigh conflicting, hallucinatory examples.<cite id="7240312b-0">XSum provides human annotations for faithfulness and factuality on 500 texts; FRANK aggregates 2,250 summaries with factuality annotations to benchmark models</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-2">FactCC provides expert-annotated validation/test splits and a synthetic portion for training inconsistency detectors</cite>.
- Apply automated, scalable verifiers as weak labels (e.g., entity-level entailment or posterior probabilities) to triage large corpora before training.<cite id="3e837f81-0">Entity-level classifiers using masked language model priors/posteriors detect hallucinated entities and improve factuality when used as rewards</cite>.

## 2) Train with verifiable references and citations
Requiring explicit attribution to source spans reduces unfaithful content and makes summaries user-verifiable. Synthetic data pipelines can bootstrap such training when labels are scarce.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Citation-grounded summarization forces models to attribute claims to source text; we propose synthetic data generation with automated verification to train grounded models, yielding an 84% LLM-as-judge accuracy vs. 43–56% for baselines while supporting very long documents</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Prior work leverages citations to construct summaries (cluster/score citation-linked sentences), though relying solely on citations may omit context; combining citations with citation-context mitigates this</cite><cite id="66e8e430-4">Citation-context and citation-network-aware methods capture contributions and link citing/ cited sentences; LLMs enhance feature extraction and pairing for citation-based summarization</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Augment training with labeled or synthetically verified claim→supporting-span pairs; constrain decoding to only summarize information supported by cited spans.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Synthetic teacher-generated data with automated verification enables training citation-grounded models at scale</cite>.
- Prefer datasets with rich structural signals (e.g., scientific discourse, citation graphs) to learn when and how to cite for verifiability.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Citations help select central claims, but must be complemented with context to avoid omitting circumstances and assumptions</cite>.

## 3) Reduce copying hallucinations via architecture and training signals
Pointer/coverage mechanisms curb extractiveness but can still over-copy long spans; structured representations and explicit selection improve abstractiveness and faithfulness.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Pointer-generator mixes copy and generate distributions and introduces a coverage loss to penalize repeated attention, reducing repetition and improving ROUGE</cite><cite id="c310bff1-2">Coverage maintains a cumulative attention vector to avoid revisiting the same source words, discouraging repetition</cite><cite id="c310bff1-3">Despite enabling abstraction, pointer-generator models often copy whole sentences; StructSum reduces copied-sequence length by 9.13 words on average and increases novel n-grams by 14.7% while matching task performance</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Add explicit content-selection layers or structured encodings (e.g., discourse/argument structure) and train with selection masks so the generator must justify content it introduces.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Bottom-up pipelines first select relevant source spans (sequence tagging) then summarize over masked relevant content</cite>.
- Use coverage regularization and copy-penalties during training; add token-level hallucination detection losses to discourage unsupported copying.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Coverage loss effectively eliminates repetition and improves ROUGE</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-3">Token-level detection of hallucinations can be done “for free” during generation, enabling joint summarization and self-check with minimal overhead</cite>.

## 4) Learn from factuality signals: entity-level rewards and attribute/claim supervision
Entity-level and attribute-level supervision targets a major driver of hallucinations—spurious new entities or claims not grounded in evidence.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Approximately 30% of entities in state-of-the-art summaries are hallucinated; over half of these hallucinated entities are factual (document/world knowledge), so entity-level supervision can substantially improve factuality</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">An automatic Entity Hallucination Index (EHI) focuses on named-entity faithfulness and can serve as a scalable reward for RL fine-tuning, promoting entity-grounded summarization without additional human labels</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Train with entity/attribute-level reward models (EHI, masked LM-based posterior priors) and use RL or reward-weighted sampling to favor faithful entity usage.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level reward signals improve factuality classification and hallucination detection, and improve summarization factuality when used for guidance</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-1">EHI-based reward fine-tuning promotes entity-grounded summarization without extra supervision, outperforming coarse factuality rewards</cite>.
- Incorporate NLI-based inconsistency detection to flag claims conflicting with source facts and use it to reweight training losses or constrain hypothesis space.<cite id="3e837f8a-2">NLI-based inconsistency detectors (e.g., Polytope categories; SUMMAC Conv trained on FactCC-derived data) label inconsistent summaries and can be trained on synthetic inconsistencies</cite>.

## 5) Use faithfulness-aware objectives and evaluation to guide data-centric improvements
Training without faithfulness signals can improve ROUGE while increasing hallucinations; thus, optimize for semantic-level faithfulness and measure both automatic and human metrics.<cite id="7240312b-2">Pretraining improves faithfulness but remains far from solving hallucination; ROUGE/BERTScore are insufficient—semantic inference metrics better capture true quality</cite>.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Pretraining improves faithfulness on future data but can also hallucinate outdated information based on parametric knowledge, demonstrating trade-offs between temporal generalization and veracity</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Co-train with factuality rewards (EHI, entity posterior priors) and faithfulness objectives (semantic inference/QuestEval/FEQA-like signals) to reduce hallucinations without harming coverage or ROUGE too much.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">Entity-level rewards reduce entity hallucinations and can be integrated directly into training</cite>.
- Evaluate with FRANK, FactCC, and domain-specific hallucination suites to ensure reductions generalize beyond ROUGE.<cite id="7240312b-0">FRANK benchmarks factuality across models by generating and annotating summaries, complementing XSum hallucination resources</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-2">FactCC provides expert-labeled splits and synthetic data for training/evaluating inconsistency detection</cite>.

## 6) Curriculum and domain adaptation: select, then summarize
Training with explicit selection of relevant content reduces hallucinations by constraining the generator to source subsets and improving abstractiveness and faithfulness.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Content selection (sequence tagging) chooses relevant source tokens and masks irrelevant parts, preventing the model from copying extraneous content</cite>.<cite id="3e837f8a-3">CNN/DailyMail exhibits fewer training-time hallucinations than XSum; token-level detection combined with repurposed factuality datasets improves precision-recall trade-offs for hallucination detection</cite>.

Actionable steps:
- Pre-train selection modules to identify key spans and train summarizers with span-masks that enforce summarization over selected content only.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Bottom-up summarization: select relevant tokens first, then summarize under the mask</cite>.
- For scientific/citation-rich domains, train with citation-context discourse models that learn when to cite and how much context to include for faithful verification.<cite id="66e8e430-3">Citations alone may omit context; combining citation content with discourse structure better reflects the original paper’s evidence and assumptions</cite>.

# What to expect: measured effects and trade-offs
- Direct reductions in hallucination prevalence and improved factuality metrics: entity-level filtering and rewards reduce hallucinated entities and factuality errors, including on XSum and related datasets.<cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level supervision reduces hallucinated entities and improves overall factuality when used as a reward</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-1">Entity-Hallucination Index-based RL fine-tuning promotes entity-grounded summarization</cite>.
- Improved abstractiveness and reduced extractive copying: structured representations and content-selection reduce long-copy spans and increase novel n-grams while preserving quality.<cite id="c310bff1-3">StructSum reduces copied sequence length by 9.13 words and increases novel trigrams by 21% vs. pointer-generator, matching task performance</cite>.
- Trade-offs with recall and ROUGE: aggressive filtering and purely extractive biases can hurt coverage and scores; balanced curricula and hybrid objectives mitigate these losses.<cite id="66e8e430-0">Entity-precision filtering (XSum→24.6% data) reduces hallucinations but drops ROUGE 8–18% and entity recall 20%, stressing the need for curriculum that preserves task knowledge</cite><cite id="66e8e430-1">CaPE leverages both clean and noisy data and reduces hallucinations without significant ROUGE or recall drops</cite>.
- Long-term reliability and verifiability: citation-grounded training with synthetic verification yields higher adjudicated accuracy and enables auditing for very long documents.<cite id="66e8e430-2">A 24B grounded model achieves 84% LLM-as-judge accuracy vs. 43–56% for open-weight baselines and can summarize texts up to 2M tokens with reliable attribution</cite>.

# Practical checklist for data-centric hallucination mitigation
- Audit your training corpus: stratify by faithfulness/factuality labels; identify noisy/conflicting examples; apply entity-level verifiers as weak labels.<cite id="7240312b-0">Human-annotated hallucination resources (XSum, FRANK) and FactCC enable targeted filtering and benchmarking</cite><cite id="3e837f8a-0">Entity-level classifiers using masked LM posteriors improve detection and can guide data triage</cite>.
- Add verifiable references: include span-level citations in training and constrain decoding to cited content; synthesize with automated verifiers when ground truth is scarce.<cite id="66e8e430-2">Synthetic data with automated verification trains citation-grounded models; explicit attribution enables user verification</cite>.
- Teach the model what to copy and when not to: train content selection layers and coverage penalties; prefer pointer/coverage variants and structured representations to curb long-copy spans.<cite id="c310bff1-0">Coverage loss reduces repetition; bottom-up selection masks irrelevant content</cite><cite id="c310bff1-3">Structured encodings reduce sentence-level copying and increase novel n-grams</cite>.
- Optimize with faithfulness rewards: integrate entity/attribute-level rewards (EHI, posterior priors) into the loss or RL curriculum; evaluate with FRANK/FactCC and semantic-inference metrics.<cite id="3e837f8a-1">EHI provides a scalable, entity-focused reward to reduce hallucinations</cite><cite id="7240312b-2">Semantic-inference metrics better capture faithfulness than ROUGE</cite>.
- Balance quality: monitor information recall, ROUGE, and novelty; use contrastive ensembling or curriculum mixing of clean/noisy data to retain diversity while reducing hallucinations.<cite id="66e8e430-1">Contrastive parameter ensembling leverages clean and noisy samples to reduce hallucinations with limited ROUGE/recall degradation</cite>.

# Summary

Our main conclusions are as follows: First, intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations happen frequently -in more than 70% of single-sentence summaries. Second, the majority of hallucinations are extrinsic, which potentially could be valid abstractions that use background knowledge. However, our study found that over 90% of extrinsic hallucinations were erroneous. Thus, hallucinations happen in most summaries and the majority of these are neither faithful nor factual. Third, models initialized with pretrained parameters perform best both on automatic metrics and human judgments of faithfulness/factuality. Furthermore, they have the highest percentage of extrinsic hallucinations that are factual. Title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We conducted a large-scale study of hallucinations in abstractive document summarization. We found that (i) tackling hallucination is a critical challenge for abstractive summarization, perhaps the most critical, (ii) NLU-driven pretraining in neural text generators is key to generate informative, coherent, faithful and factual abstracts, but it is still far from solving the problem; and (iii) measures such as ROUGE or BERTScore will not be sufficient when studying the problem; semantic inference-based automatic measures are better representations of true summarization quality.

Title: Towards Attribute-Entangled Controllable Text Generation: A Pilot Study of Blessing Generation
Snippet: Hallucinations in abstractive summarization are model generations that are unfaithful to the source document. Current methods for detecting hallucinations operate mostly on noun phrases and named entities, and restrict themselves to the XSum dataset, which is known to have hallucinations in 3 out of 4 training examples (Maynez et al., 2020). We instead consider the CNN/DailyMail dataset where the summarization model has not seen abnormally many hallucinations during training. We automatically detect candidate hallucinations at the token level, irrespective of its part of speech. Our detection comes essentially for free, as we only use information the model already produces during generation of the summary. This enables practitioners to jointly generate a summary and identify possible hallucinations, with minimal overhead. We repurpose an existing factuality dataset and create our own token-level annotations. The evaluation on these two datasets shows that our model achieves better precision-recall tradeoffs than its competitors, which additionally require a model forward pass.

Title: Hallucinated but Factual! Inspecting the Factuality of Hallucinations in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: In this paper, we investigate the hallucination and factuality problems in abstractive summarization. We show that about 30% of entities generated by state-of-the-art summarization model are hallucinated. More interestingly, more than half of the hallucinated entities are factual with respect to the source document and world knowledge. We propose a novel method based on the entity's prior and posterior probabilities according to masked language models. Our approach outperforms five base-  Table 7: Comparison of different summarization models. Results are evaluated on XSUM's official test set. "% Factual Ent" and "% Factual Hal" are the percentage of factual entities and factual hallucinations classified by ENTFA model respectively. "% ENFS" is the percentage of entities in generated summary that not found in source document. For the loss truncation baseline, c is the percentage of data to be dropped.    line models on both factuality classification and hallucination detection tasks on human-annotated datasets. In addition, using our classifier as a reward signal vastly improves the factuality of summarization systems. Our approach is limited to entity-level hallucination and factuality classification. In the future, we are interested in extending our work to arbitrary text spans.

Title: Reducing Hallucinations in Summarization via Reinforcement Learning with Entity Hallucination Index
Snippet: Hallucination in Summarization. Hallucination, or the generation of content that is unfaithful to the input, is a long-standing challenge in abstractive summarization (Maynez et al., 2020). Several studies have quantified hallucination prevalence across datasets and models (Pagnoni et al., 2021). Techniques such as constrained decoding (Cao et al., 2020) and fact-checking-based reranking (Goyal et al., 2022) have been proposed to mitigate hallucination during or after generation. 

Entity-Level Hallucination Detection. Prior work has recognized the importance of entity-level evaluation for factuality. Metrics like FEQA (Durmus et al., 2020) and QuestEval (Scialom et al., 2021) attempt to assess factual consistency using question answering techniques. However, these methods often require reference summaries or external QA systems, limiting scalability. Our work builds on this line by employing the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI), a lightweight evaluation metric focusing specifically on named entity faithfulness. 

Reward-Driven Fine-Tuning. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has gained traction for aligning model outputs with desired qualities, such as factuality and helpfulness (Ouyang et al., 2022). In summarization, factualityaware reward models have been used for finetuning (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018). Unlike previous approaches that rely on coarse factuality rewards or human-labeled datasets, we propose finetuning using EHI as a direct, automatic reward signal, thereby promoting entity-grounded summarization without additional supervision.

Title: SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization
Snippet: (eXtreme Summarization Faithfulness, XSF) (Maynez et al., 2020) is a dataset with models trained on the XSum dataset (Narayan et al., 2018) which consists of more abstractive summaries than CoGenSumm. The authors find that standard generators remain consistent for only 20-30% of generated summaries. The authors differentiate between extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations (which we call inconsistencies in this work). Extrinsic hallucinations, which involve words or concepts not in the original document can nonetheless be accurate or inaccurate. In order for a summarizer to generate an accurate extrinsic hallucination, the summarizer must possess external world knowledge. Because the authors found that the models are primarily inaccurate in terms of extrinsic hallucinations, we map both extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations to a common inconsistent label. 

Polytope (Huang et al., 2020) introduces a more extensive typology of summarization errors, based on the Multi-dimensional Quality Metric (Mariana, 2014). Each summary is annotated with eight possible errors, as well as a severity level for the error. We standardize this dataset by labeling a summary as inconsistent if it was annotated with any of the five accuracy errors (and disregarded the three fluency errors). Each summary in Polytope was labeled by a single annotator, making it impossible to measure inter-annotator agreement. 

FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020) contains validation and test splits that are entirely annotated by authors of the paper, because attempts at crowdsourced annotation yielded low inter-annotator agreement. Prior work (Gillick and Liu, 2010) shows that there can be divergence in annotations between experts and non-experts in summarization, and because the authors of the pa-per are NLP researchers familiar with the limitations of automatic summarizations, we expect that FactCC annotations differs in quality from other datasets. FactCC also introduces a synthetic dataset by modifying consistent summaries with semantically variant rules. We use a sub-portion of this synthetic dataset to train the SUMMAC Conv model.

Title: Automatic Evaluation of Attribution by Large Language Models
Snippet: Summarization involves condensing a given passage or article into brief sentences while preserving its original meaning. To simulate contradictory examples, we use datasets with annotations of hallucinations. In terms of XSum-Hallucination (Maynez et al., 2020), we merge examples with the same ID and consider those with the most intrinsic hallucination as contradictory and those with the most extrinsic hallucination as extrapolatory. Paired full articles and ground truth summaries are treated as attributable examples. For XENT (Cao et al., 2022), 'Non-factual Hallucination' and 'Intrinsic Hallucination' are seen as contradictory, 'Factual Hallucination' as extrapolatory, and 'Non-hallucinated' as attributable. Each article and reference are paired as attributable examples. Finally, we resplit the manually annotated dev and test sets for training and evaluation in FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020), with 'INCORRECT' labeled as extrapolatory and 'CORRECT' as attributable.

The authors differentiate between extrinsic and intrinsic hallucinations (which we call inconsistencies in this work). Extrinsic hallucinations, which involve words or concepts not in the original document can nonetheless be accurate or inaccurate. snippet.text: Hallucinations in abstractive summarization are model generations that are unfaithful to the source document. Current methods for detecting hallucinations operate mostly on noun phrases and named entities, and restrict themselves to the XSum dataset, which is known to have hallucinations in 3 out of 4 training examples (Maynez et al., 2020). We instead consider the CNN/DailyMail dataset where the summarization model has not seen abnormally many hallucinations during training. We automatically detect candidate hallucinations at the token level, irrespective of its part of speech. Our detection comes essentially for free, as we only use information the model already produces during generation of the summary. This enables practitioners to jointly generate a summary and identify possible hallucinations, with minimal overhead. We repurpose an existing factuality dataset and create our own token-level annotations. The evaluation on these two datasets shows that our model achieves better precision-recall tradeoffs than its competitors, which additionally require a model forward pass.

documents.title: Reducing Hallucinations in Summarization via Reinforcement Learning with Entity Hallucination Index
documents.snippet:
Hallucination in Summarization. Hallucination, or the generation of content that is unfaithful to the input, is a long-standing challenge in abstractive summarization (Maynez et al., 2020). Several studies have quantified hallucination prevalence across datasets and models (Pagnoni et al., 2021). Techniques such as constrained decoding (Cao et al., 2020) and fact-checking-based reranking (Goyal et al., 2022) have been proposed to mitigate hallucination during or after generation. 

Entity-Level Hallucination Detection. Prior work has recognized the importance of entity-level evaluation for factuality. Metrics like FEQA (Durmus et al., 2020) and QuestEval (Scialom et al., 2021) attempt to assess factual consistency using question answering techniques. However, these methods often require reference summaries or external QA systems, limiting scalability. Our work builds on this line by employing the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI), a lightweight evaluation metric focusing specifically on named entity faithfulness. 

Reward-Driven Fine-Tuning. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has gained traction for aligning model outputs with desired qualities, such as factuality and helpfulness (Ouyang et al., 2022). In summarization, factualityaware reward models have been used for finetuning (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018). Unlike previous approaches that rely on coarse factuality rewards or human-labeled datasets, we propose finetuning using EHI as a direct, automatic reward signal, thereby promoting entity-grounded summarization without additional supervision.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Neural abstractive summarization systems have been shown to generate plausible summaries with high lexical overlap with the references. However, human analyses (Fabbri et al., 2021a;Pagnoni et al., 2021;Tejaswin et al., 2021) and automatic evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2020;Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020) show that state-of-the-art models trained on the widely used XSUM (Narayan et al., 2018) and CNN/DM (Hermann et al., 2015)   information with high frequency. The degree of a model's hallucinations further correlates with the quality of the training data (Aralikatte et al., 2021;Pagnoni et al., 2021). For instance, models trained on the XSum data tend to generate a higher proportion of factual errors as compared to models trained on the CNN/DM dataset. 

Given the association between training data quality and hallucinations in resulting models, the easiest method to reduce hallucinations is to remove noisy samples from the training data (Nan et al., 2021). However, data filtering reduces the size of training data and consequently, the diversity in target summary since the removed noisy samples might also include useful task-specific knowledge. This impacts other aspects of the generated summaries such as information recall or fluency. In Table 1, we show ROUGE (R-1/2/L) and named entity recall (E-R ref ) with respect to the reference summary of a BART model (Lewis et al., 2020) trained on the entity precision-filtered XSUM data (24.6% of the original data). The new model drops 8-18% in ROUGE and 20% drop in entity recall. 

In this work, we design a simple yet effective strategy to utilize both clean and noisy training samples.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We present Contrastive Parameter Ensembling (CaPE) to reduce content hallucinations in abstractive summarization models. We first select clean (noisy) training samples to fine-tune an expert (antiexpert) model. Then, we use the difference between the parameters of expert and anti-expert models to adjust the parameters of a base summarization model. We evaluate CaPE on the XSUM and CNN/DM datasets using a diverse set of factual metrics, finding that CaPE effectively reduces hallucinations without a significant drop in ROUGE and information recall.

Title: sui-1: Grounded and Verifiable Long-Form Summarization
Snippet: Large language models excel at summarization but frequently generate unfaithful content, including fabricated facts or misattributed claims that users cannot trust without laboriously verifying against source documents. Citation-grounded summarization addresses this by requiring models to explicitly attribute claims to source text, enabling users to quickly assess reliability and trace claims to their origins. 

Training citation-grounded models presents challenges: standard datasets lack citation annotations, manual annotation is prohibitively expensive, and the task requires precise coordination between content generation and source reference. We address these challenges through synthetic data generation using a capable teacher model, with automated verification ensuring citation accuracy before training. 

We introduce sui-1, a 24B parameter model achieving 84% overall accuracy on LLM-as-a-judge evaluation compared to 43-56% for baselines (Figure 1). The model notably outperforms all tested open-weight baselines, demonstrating that task-specific training provides greater benefit than scale alone. sui-1 reliably processes documents exceeding 100 pages, with iterative chunking enabling summarization of texts up to 2 million tokens.

Title: Scientific Article Summarization Using Citation-Context and Article’s Discourse Structure
Snippet: Training the discourse parser requires large amount of training data in the RST framework. 

Scientific article summarization was first studied by Teufel and Moens (2002) in which they trained a supervised Naive Bayes classifier to select informative content for the summary. Later Elkiss et al. (2008) argue the benefits of citations to scientific work analysis. Cohan et al. (2015) use a search oriented approach for finding relevant parts of the reference paper to citations. Qazvinian and Radev (2008;Qazvinian et al. (2013) use citations to an article to construct its summary. More specifically, they perform hierarchical agglomerative clustering on citations to maximize purity and select most central sentences from each cluster for the final summary. Our work is closest to Qazvinian and Radev (2008) with the difference that they only make use of citations. While citations are useful for summarization, relying solely on them might not accurately capture the original context of the referenced paper. That is, the generated summary lacks the appropriate evidence to reflect the content of the original paper, such as circumstances, data and assumptions under which certain findings were obtained. We address this shortcoming by leveraging the citation-context and the inherent discourse model in the scientific articles.

Title: When Large Language Models Meet Citation: A Survey
Snippet: Aggregating all citation sentences referring to a paper can yield a significant amount of information about the paper itself (Abu-Jbara and Radev, 2011). Citation-based summarization harnesses the citations from a scientific article or its reference citation network to assemble a succinct summary. The summary aims to highlight the main contributions of papers, based on citation sentences from papers that cite the source document. The initial attempt uses sentence clustering and ranking methods (Luo et al., 2023). 

With the progression of research, automatic citation-based summarization can be broadly divided into two distinct categories as follows: (a) document-level citation context span based summarization (Qazvinian and Radev, 2008). Techniques involving span identification and varied feature extraction have been utilized (Cohan and Goharian, 2015); (b) citation network structured aware summarization. More recent research works put forward the idea that citation graphs can be instrumental in creating top-notch summaries of scientific papers (Chen et al., 2022;Luo et al., 2023). LLMs, with their proficiency in deriving complex text representations from dense vectors and generating high-quality text, are gaining prominence in complex tasks like citation-based summarization. Hence, there's an enhanced capability to encode citation context and integrate citation network graphs, thereby further boosting citation-based summarization efforts (Luo et al., 2023). Document-level Features. Given their superior capability to derive text representation from textual input, LLMs can be employed for capturing document-level features within a citation recommendation system. Saini et al. (2023) introduce a multi-view clustering approach that utilizes dualembedding spaces and citation contexts for document summarization, leveraging document encoders like BERT, GPT-2, and XLNET to capture document-level features. Roy and Mercer (2022) propose a method for establishing connections between citing sentences and corresponding citation sentences in the referred literature. Their framework pairs every sentence in a publication with all sentences from the referenced document, then seeks to identify semantically similar pairs. The selected sentences from the referenced paper, which have semantic similarities with the publication's sentences, are considered cited statements.

Document-level Features. Given their superior capability to derive text representation from textual input, LLMs can be employed for capturing document-level features within a citation recommendation system. Saini et al. (2023) introduce a multi-view clustering approach that utilizes dualembedding spaces and citation contexts for document summarization, leveraging document encoders like BERT, GPT-2, and XLNET to capture document-level features. Roy and Mercer (2022) propose a method for establishing connections between citing sentences and corresponding citation sentences in the referred literature. Their framework pairs every sentence in a publication with all sentences from the referenced document, then seeks to identify semantically similar pairs. The selected sentences from the referenced paper, which have semantic similarities with the publication's sentences, are considered cited statements.
