Summary answer
- Short answer: Yes—many interventions that reduce hallucinations in abstractive summarization also reduce abstractiveness, pushing outputs toward more extractive, source-verbatim behavior; however, this is not universal, and several methods explicitly tune or trade off abstraction to improve faithfulness while preserving quality. The trade-off is clearest when models are constrained to avoid unsupported content (e.g., via entity-level rewards or controlled copying), which increases copying and reduces abstract paraphrase but improves factuality; conversely, semantic or novelty-aware rewards can increase abstractiveness while reducing repetition, at the cost of risking more subtle hallucinations if safeguards are not maintained. <cite id="9653de1c-3">The degree of abstractiveness affects factuality inversely: extractive summaries copy more phrases and tend to be more factual, whereas higher abstraction can correlate with higher hallucination and, in some cases, lower ROUGE</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-0">Abstractive systems frequently hallucinate content unsupported by the source even when ROUGE is high</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-1">Even summaries with substantial hallucinations can score highly on ROUGE, motivating faithfulness-focused mitigation</cite> <cite id="299da30b-0">Controlling copying provides a knob to increase or decrease abstraction; reducing copying reduces hallucinations but lowers abstractiveness</cite> <cite id="299da30b-4">Rewarding semantic closeness plus novelty can improve abstractiveness and reduce repetition, illustrating that boosting abstraction need not increase hallucinations if paired with semantic guidance</cite>.

Background: hallucination prevalence and evaluation pitfalls
- Abstractive summarization models often hallucinate content not supported by the source, yet such summaries can achieve high ROUGE scores; this mismatch undermines trust and necessitates faithfulness-aware interventions. <cite id="6c209bf8-0">64.1% of XSum summaries from a BERT-based abstractive model were found to contain hallucinations</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-1">Studies report large proportions of hallucinated content in SOTA systems, and high ROUGE despite hallucinations, spurring work on hallucination-aware evaluation and mitigation</cite>. 
- ROUGE measures lexical overlap and can miss factuality or hallucinations; richer metrics (BERTScore, semantic inference/entailment, human judgments) better capture faithfulness and quality dimensions like informativeness, fluency, and succinctness. <cite id="9653de1c-1">ROUGE or BERTScore are insufficient alone; semantic inference-based metrics better represent true summarization quality</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human evaluations capture informativeness, fluency, and succinctness, complementing ROUGE</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-3">Human annotations of intrinsic/extrinsic hallucinations and factuality reveal that high ROUGE does not guarantee faithful summaries</cite>.

Evidence that anti-hallucination pushes summaries toward extractiveness
- Interventions that bias against unsupported content (e.g., entity-level rewards, controlled copying) increase copying and reduce abstract paraphrase, improving factuality but lowering abstractiveness and sometimes ROUGE. <cite id="299da30b-0">Methods that control copying can increase or decrease abstraction; when copying is discouraged, summaries become less abstract and more faithful to the source, with evaluations via ROUGE, BERTScore, and human assessments</cite> <cite id="299da30b-3">EHI-guided RL reduces entity hallucinations by rewarding entity-grounded generation; this directly favors copying or cautious paraphrase of grounded content, improving entity faithfulness</cite>. 
- Empirically, augmenting training data to be counterfactual or more specific improves factuality but yields a measurable trade-off in abstraction: in XSum, about 9% of samples are “factually correct with reduced ROUGE,” with qualitative analysis showing models copy more like extractive baselines to avoid hallucinations and that extractive summaries tend to be more factual. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Counterfactual augmentation improved factuality; across sampled outputs, 9% were factually correct with reduced ROUGE because models adopted more extractive copying; extractive summaries are often more factual than abstractive ones, indicating an inverse relation between abstractiveness and factuality</cite>. 
- Human-centered analyses and surveys converge on the mechanism: abstract paraphrase enables novel expression but risks fabrication; higher copying is more faithful but can reduce fluency/readability and ROUGE relative to references. <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human judgments emphasize informativeness, fluency, and succinctness, highlighting quality dimensions affected when models become more extractive</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-2">Abstractive models’ hallucinations are prevalent, and ROUGE can overestimate quality; improving hallucination evaluation motivates interventions that curb abstraction</cite>.

Training-time interventions: data and reward design
- Data augmentation and curriculum: Counterfactual augmentation and specificity-focused training improve factuality by conditioning models to include entity-level evidence; however, in some cases this reduces ROUGE because the model avoids unsupported paraphrase and copies source phrases more often. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Augmented data make models more specific; 9% of samples improved factuality but reduced ROUGE; qualitative inspection shows models adopt more extractive copying to avoid hallucinations</cite>. 
- Entity-level reinforcement learning: Rewarding entity faithfulness (EHI) reduces hallucinated entities and improves factuality; because the reward grounds entities in the input, the model is steered toward copying or cautious paraphrase of grounded content, which reduces abstractiveness of entity-bearing spans. <cite id="299da30b-3">EHI-guided RL improves entity faithfulness across meeting summarization datasets, indicating models produce entity-grounded outputs that penalize unsupported lexical abstraction</cite>. 
- Hybrid objectives and semantic control: Some RL frameworks explicitly combine semantic similarity with novelty to maintain abstractiveness while reducing repetition, showing that boosting abstraction need not increase hallucination if semantic guidance is present. <cite id="299da30b-4">Integrating cosine similarity and word mover’s distance with ROUGE-L yields summaries that are semantically close yet novel, improving abstractiveness and reducing grammatical issues compared to baselines</cite>.

Decoding-time interventions: copy/faithfulness constraints
- Controllable copying: Methods that expose and regulate a model’s copy mechanism can explicitly increase or decrease the proportion of verbatim copying at decoding time, yielding a spectrum of summaries between extractive and highly abstract; reducing copying at decoding reduces hallucinations but also reduces abstractiveness. <cite id="299da30b-0">Copying can be controlled during training and decoding; varying seen/unseen summary word proportions and search/reranking strategies allows generating summaries with different amounts of copied content, evaluated via ROUGE, BERTScore, and human grammaticality/informativeness/true-to-original assessments</cite>. 
- Faithfulness-aware decoding: RL or entity-index-driven decoding directly penalizes unsupported content; these approaches often increase the likelihood of copying grounded spans and thus lower abstractiveness in entity-laden regions, improving entity-level faithfulness. <cite id="299da30b-3">Entity Hallucination Index RL penalizes unsupported entities, steering generation toward entity-grounded copying or conservative paraphrase</cite>. 
- Trade-off calibration: Because ROUGE can overestimate quality of hallucinated content, decoding strategies that incorporate faithfulness or semantic similarity metrics avoid overestimating gains; this clarifies why “less abstract” outputs may appear lower in ROUGE but higher in factuality/faithfulness metrics. <cite id="9653de1c-1">Semantic inference metrics better capture faithfulness than ROUGE</cite> <cite id="299da30b-2">BERTScore and entailment-based metrics reflect meaning rather than lexical overlap, reducing ROUGE’s overestimation of abstract but hallucinated content</cite>.

Retrieval-augmented summarization (RAG) and the abstraction–hallucination seesaw
- RAG pipelines reduce hallucinations by constraining generation to retrieved evidence; however, ROUGE-based overlap metrics penalize divergence from references, so ROUGE can decline even as faithfulness improves; replacing or supplementing ROUGE with faithfulness/semantic metrics reveals true gains. <cite id="299da30b-2">As retrieved chunks increase, ROUGE recall declines while BERTScore F1 and RAGA faithfulness/relevancy stabilize or improve, indicating that semantic/faithfulness metrics better capture correct, grounded generation beyond lexical overlap</cite>. 
- In practice, RAG can preserve or even increase abstractiveness by paraphrasing retrieved content, provided the retriever covers needed facts; when coverage is incomplete, models may hallucinate, and the system’s faithfulness checks trigger retrieval or constrain copying, nudging outputs toward extractive phrasing of retrieved spans. <cite id="299da30b-2">RAG pipelines emphasize faithfulness and semantic similarity over ROUGE recall to avoid penalizing semantically correct divergence and to surface hallucinations missed by ROUGE</cite>. 
- Human evaluations in RAG-summarization workflows consistently find that faithful grounded outputs are preferred over fluent hallucinated ones, reinforcing that interventions which increase grounding (and sometimes copying) reduce hallucinations at the cost of stylistic abstraction. <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human judgments prioritize informativeness and grammaticality but also assess true-to-original faithfulness, aligning with interventions that increase copying/grounding</cite>.

Resolving the trade-off: mechanisms, metrics, and design principles
- Mechanism: Abstract paraphrase expands lexical novelty but increases the surface area for unsupported content; controlled copying and entity-level constraints shrink novelty in source-grounded regions to prevent hallucinations. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Inverse relation between abstractiveness and factuality: extractive copying is more factual; higher abstraction correlates with more hallucinations and sometimes lower ROUGE</cite> <cite id="299da30b-0">Copying control provides explicit levers to trade abstract paraphrase for faithfulness</cite>. 
- Metrics: Use ROUGE to monitor lexical overlap and readability, but complement with entity/faithfulness metrics (EHI, BERTScore, entailment QA) and human factuality/faithfulness judgments to detect hallucinations and calibrate abstraction levels. <cite id="9653de1c-1">Semantic inference metrics better represent true quality than ROUGE alone</cite> <cite id="299da30b-3">Entity Hallucination Index quantifies entity-level faithfulness for training and evaluation</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human assessments capture informativeness, fluency, succinctness, and true-to-original faithfulness</cite>. 
- Design patterns that manage trade-offs:
  - Knob-based control: Expose copying probabilities or semantic-novelty penalties so operators can tune abstractiveness for domain risk (e.g., legal/medical). <cite id="299da30b-0">Controlled copying yields a spectrum of summaries; operators can favor or disfavor copying depending on needs</cite> <cite id="299da30b-4">Semantics-plus-novelty rewards improve abstractiveness while reducing repetition</cite>.
  - Curriculum and augmentation: Train with counterfactual or specific evidence to encourage faithful paraphrase without forcing extractiveness globally; monitor ROUGE to quantify readability impact. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Counterfactual augmentation improved factuality with some samples showing reduced ROUGE due to more extractive copying</cite>.
  - Retrieval-first: Use RAG with faithfulness checks to maintain abstractiveness where possible while constraining hallucinations via grounded evidence; avoid ROUGE-only optimization. <cite id="299da30b-2">RAG pipelines favor faithfulness and semantic similarity metrics over ROUGE recall to reflect grounded, semantically correct outputs</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- If your primary risk is factual correctness (e.g., meetings, legal docs), prefer interventions that penalize unsupported content and increase copying/grounding; expect lower abstractiveness and possibly lower ROUGE, but higher factuality and human preference. <cite id="299da30b-3">Entity-level RL reduces hallucinations by steering generation toward entity-grounded content</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-3">More extractive copying often yields more factual outputs, improving factuality at the cost of ROUGE</cite>. 
- If you need high ROUGE/readability while controlling hallucinations, combine semantic similarity rewards with coverage/pointer mechanisms to expand paraphrase while maintaining evidence links; validate with entailment/faithfulness metrics and human factuality checks. <cite id="299da30b-4">Semantic similarity plus novelty rewards can improve abstractiveness and reduce repetition</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-1">Entailment/semantic metrics detect hallucinations missed by ROUGE</cite>. 
- Always ablate both ends: measure how faithfulness gains from anti-hallucination methods shift ROUGE-A/L, copying ratio, and human-rated abstractiveness/faithfulness to quantify the trade-off for your dataset. <cite id="299da30b-0">Human and automatic multi-metric evaluations (ROUGE, BERTScore) reveal when copying control trades abstractiveness for faithfulness</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human judgments provide grounded assessments of informativeness, fluency, succinctness, and true-to-original faithfulness</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
- Dataset dependence: Some corpora may reward abstract paraphrase more strongly than others; interventions that reduce hallucinations can still preserve abstraction if references are strong or if retrieval coverage is high. <cite id="9653de1c-2">ROUGE is widely used but insufficient; dataset-specific factuality patterns require faithfulness-aware evaluation</cite>. 
- Granularity: Entity-level metrics capture coarse entity hallucinations but miss fine-grained factual errors; combining multiple metrics and human checks mitigates this. <cite id="299da30b-3">EHI targets entity hallucinations and improves entity faithfulness</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-1">Semantic inference-based metrics better capture faithfulness than token overlap</cite>. 
- Future directions: RL and data augmentation show clear trade-offs; more work directly optimizing a multi-objective of abstractiveness, faithfulness, and readability on large document corpora with human-in-the-loop adjudication would further resolve the balance. <cite id="6c209bf8-1">Surveys emphasize improving hallucination evaluation and mitigation while acknowledging remaining challenges</cite>.

In sum, evidence across multiple studies shows that training- and decoding-time interventions which curb hallucinations typically reduce abstractiveness by increasing copying or constraining paraphrase; extractive or entity-grounded outputs improve factuality but often underperform on ROUGE and human readability, whereas semantic/controlled abstraction methods can preserve more paraphrase while limiting hallucinations when paired with faithfulness signals. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Reduced ROUGE alongside improved factuality appears when models adopt more extractive copying to avoid hallucinations</cite> <cite id="299da30b-0">Copying control offers explicit tuning between abstraction and faithfulness</cite> <cite id="299da30b-4">Semantic novelty guidance can increase abstractiveness while reducing repetition, avoiding a pure abstraction loss</cite>. The trade-off is not inescapable—careful metric design and multi-objective training/decoding can preserve more abstraction while controlling hallucinations—but doing so requires replacing ROUGE-centric evaluation with faithfulness-aware metrics and human assessments. <cite id="9653de1c-1">ROUGE alone is insufficient; semantic inference metrics better align with true faithfulness</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human judgments capture the quality dimensions affected by the abstraction–faithfulness trade-off</cite>.

Snippet: Our initial setup included ROUGE recall (average of ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L) as one of the core metrics to evaluate content overlap with reference answers. However, as shown in Figure 4, we observe that ROUGE recall exhibits a declining trend as the number of retrieved chunks (k) increases, in contrast to metrics such as BERTScore F1 and RAGA Faithfulness/Relevancy, which stabilise or improve. This discrepancy motivated an in-depth investigation of the limitations of ROUGE in this context. 

ROUGE was originally designed to evaluate extractive summarization by computing n-gram overlap between generated and reference texts (Chalkidis et al., 2020). While effective for summarisation and simple question-answering scenarios, it falls short in evaluating abstractive or semantically equivalent generation, especially when the wording differs from the reference but the meaning is preserved. Hence, for more meaningful and context-aware evaluation, we focus on RAGAS Faithfulness and Relevancy, which accounts for whether the answer is grounded in retrieved content; BERTScore F1 (Exploding Gradients, 2025), which reflects semantic similarity at the embedding level. By excluding ROUGE recall, we avoid penalising correct responses that diverge lexically, and better align our evaluation metrics with the goals of faithful and relevant generation.

Title: Reducing Hallucinations in Summarization via Reinforcement Learning with Entity Hallucination Index
Snippet: Abstractive summarization models, powered by large language models (LLMs), have achieved impressive results across various domains. However, a persistent challenge remains: hallucination, where generated summaries include incorrect or fabricated information not grounded in the source input (Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020). In high-stakes applications such as meeting summarization, medical reporting, or financial documentation, hallucinations, particularly involving named entities, can significantly undermine trustworthiness and utility. 

Existing work on hallucination detection primarily focuses on coarse-grained factuality metrics or relies on reference-based evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Pagnoni et al., 2021). While such methods are valuable, they often fail to capture fine-grained entity-level hallucinations, and their dependence on ground-truth references limits scalability. Recent efforts have explored lightweight automatic metrics, yet integrating such evaluations directly into model training remains underexplored. 

In this work, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach that leverages the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI) as a reward signal to reduce hallucinations at the entity level. EHI quantifies the correctness and grounding of entities by comparing extracted entities from model outputs to those present in the input document, enabling efficient evaluation with reduced reference. We first generate baseline summaries using a pre-trained model, compute EHI scores through automatic entity extraction and matching, and fine-tune the model using reinforcement learning with EHI as the reward function. This method biases the model toward producing more entity-faithful summaries without requiring human factuality annotations. 

Our contributions are as follows: 

• We introduce an EHI-guided fine-tuning framework that improves entity faithfulness in abstractive summarization. 

• We present a scalable reinforcement learning pipeline that does not depend on humanlabeled factuality datasets. 

• We demonstrate empirical improvements in EHI scores across meeting transcript datasets and conduct qualitative analysis to highlight reductions in hallucination. 

• We release a reproducible Colab-based implementation to facilitate further research on hallucination-aware summarization.
</snippet>

Title: Abstractive text summarization: State of the art, challenges, and improvements

[97] addressed the limitations of traditional ROUGE-L based methods, which often generate repetitive summaries, by introducing two new RL reward functions: ROUGE-SIM and ROUGE-WMD. These functions integrate Cosine Similarity and Word Mover's Distance [106] respectively, with the ROUGE-L score, ensuring summaries are semantically close to the source text while promoting novelty and reducing direct copying. To generate accurate, innovative, and grammatically sound summaries, a decoding method based on these reward functions was proposed. The Gigaword dataset was employed to evaluate the new methods. The authors used three metrics: ROUGE-PACKAGE, novel n-grams, and Grammarly9 to measure summary quality, originality, and grammatical integrity. The proposed models surpassed various baselines, offering consistent performance, higher semantic value, improved abstractiveness, and reduced grammatical errors. 

Keneshloo et al. [98] introduced an RL framework for abstractive text summarization to address exposure bias and improve generalization to unfamiliar datasets. Exposure bias means that during the training phase, the model is provided with an accurate input at every decoder step, while in the testing phase, it must generate the next token based on its own output [98]. They used a Pointer-Generator [41] model combined with an RL objective and a transfer reinforcement learning approach. Traditional methods relying on cross-entropy (CE) loss often suffer from exposure bias and poor generalization. In contrast, the proposed RL objective minimizes the negative expected reward, enabling the model to train based on its own output, in line with metrics like ROUGE. This self-critical policy gradient approach emphasizes better-performing samples during training. However, the model faced challenges in transfer learning due to training on the source dataset distribution. To counter this, they introduced a transfer RL approach using a shared encoder and a trade-off parameter to balance source and target dataset training. The authors used four datasets: Newsroom [107], CNN/Daily Mail, DUC 2003 10 , and DUC 2004 11 , for training and evaluating text summarization models. They evaluated the models using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F1 scores.

- Always ablate both ends: measure how faithfulness gains from anti-hallucination methods shift ROUGE-A/L, copying ratio, and human-rated abstractiveness/faithfulness to quantify the trade-off for your dataset. <cite id="299da30b-0">Human and automatic multi-metric evaluations (ROUGE, BERTScore) reveal when copying control trades abstractiveness for faithfulness</cite> <cite id="6c209bf8-2">Human judgments provide grounded assessments of informativeness, fluency, succinctness, and true-to-original faithfulness</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
- Dataset dependence: Some corpora may reward abstract paraphrase more strongly than others; interventions that reduce hallucinations can still preserve abstraction if references are strong or if retrieval coverage is high. <cite id="9653de1c-2">ROUGE is widely used but insufficient; dataset-specific factuality patterns require faithfulness-aware evaluation</cite>. 
- Granularity: Entity-level metrics capture coarse entity hallucinations but miss fine-grained factual errors; combining multiple metrics and human checks mitigates this. <cite id="299da30b-3">EHI targets entity hallucinations and improves entity faithfulness</cite> <cite id="9653de1c-1">Semantic inference-based metrics better capture faithfulness than token overlap</cite>. 
- Future directions: RL and data augmentation show clear trade-offs; more work directly optimizing a multi-objective of abstractiveness, faithfulness, and readability on large document corpora with human-in-the-loop adjudication would further resolve the balance. <cite id="6c209bf8-1">Surveys emphasize improving hallucination evaluation and mitigation while acknowledging remaining challenges</cite>.

In sum, evidence across multiple studies shows that training- and decoding-time interventions which curb hallucinations typically reduce abstractiveness by increasing copying or constraining paraphrase; extractive or entity-grounded outputs improve factuality but often underperform on ROUGE and human readability, whereas semantic/controlled abstraction methods can preserve more paraphrase while limiting hallucinations when paired with faithfulness signals. <cite id="9653de1c-3">Reduced ROUGE alongside improved factuality appears when models adopt more extractive copying to avoid hallucinations</cite> <cite id="299da30b-0">Copying control offers explicit tuning between abstraction and faithfulness</cite> <cite id="299da30b-4">Semantic novelty guidance can increase abstractiveness while reducing repetition, avoiding a pure abstraction loss</cite>. Title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
Snippet: Abstractive summarization aims to extract essential information from source documents and to generate short, concise, and readable summaries [158]. Neural networks have achieved remarkable results on abstractive summarization. However, Maynez et al. [90] observe that neural abstractive summarization models are likely to generate hallucinatory content that is unfaithful to the source document. Falke et al. [32] analyze three recent abstractive summarization systems and show that 25% of the summaries generated from SOTA models have hallucinated content. In addition, Zhou et al. [168] mention that even if a summary contains a large amount of hallucinatory content, it can achieve a high ROUGE score. This has encouraged researchers to actively devise ways to improve the evaluation of abstractive summarization, especially from the hallucination perspective.

Title: STEP: Sequence-to-Sequence Transformer Pre-training for Document Summarization
Snippet: We used ROUGE (Lin, 2004) to measure the quality of different summarization model outputs. We reported full-length F1 based ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L scores on CN-NDM, while we used the limited-length recall based ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L on NYT following (Durrett et al., 2016). The ROUGE scores are computed using the ROUGE-1.5.5.pl script. 

Since summaries generated by abstractive models may produce disfluent or ungrammatical outputs, we also evaluated abstractive systems by eliciting human judgements. Following previous work (Cheng and Lapata, 2016;Narayan et al., 2018), 20 documents are randomly sampled from the test split of CNNDM. Title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: The main focus of this work is not to propose a solution to hallucination related issues, but to achieve a better understanding of hallucinations in abstractive summarization through their human assessment. We randomly sampled 500 articles from the test set to facilitate our study. Using the full test set was unfeasible given its size and the cost of human judgments. We have trained annotators (fluent in English) specifically for our assessment. Our annotators went through two pilot studies to have a better understanding of intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations, and factuality of summaries. Documents used in the pilot studies were not used in the final annotation. We also report on ROUGE (Lin and Hovy, 2003) scores, BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020) and semantic inference metric such as textual entailment (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018;Welleck et al., 2019;Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2019b) and question answering (Arumae and Liu, 2019;Wang et al., 2020). (Lin and Hovy, 2003) provides a means to quickly assess a model's ability to generate summaries closer to human authored summaries. We report on ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 for informativeness and ROUGE-L, for fluency. Like ROUGE, BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020) computes a similarity score for each token in the candidate sum- mary with each token in the reference summary. However, instead of exact matches, it computes token similarity using contextual embeddings. Results are presented in Table 1.

Title: A Hybrid Word-Character Model for Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We adopt ROUGE (Lin, 2004) metrics for evaluation, which has been widely used for abstractive summarization. They measure the quality of summaries by computing the overlap of systemgenerated and reference ones. For a fair comparison, we report ROUGE-1 (1-gram), ROUGE-2 (bigrams) and ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence) F1 scores for all compared methods.

Title: Controllable Summarization with Constrained Markov Decision Process
Snippet: Abstractive summarization. Most of the existing abstractive summarization models (Gehrmann et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020a;Chan et al., 2020) are built on the encoder-decoder model (Bahdanau et al., 2015) to generate summaries. See et al. (2017) propose the pointer-generator network which allows copying words from the source to the output summary. The structure-infused copy mechanism (Song et al., 2018) incorporates the syntactic structure of the source text into the pointer-generator network to facilitate copying important words to the output summary. Lebanoff et al. (2019) propose a summarization framework that first extracts either a single sentence or a pair of sentences from the source document, then it condenses or fuses the selected sentence(s) to generate a summary. The above models do not allow users to constrain the degree of copying nor sentence fusion from the source document. 

Recent methods apply RL with MDP to optimize an abstractive summarization model towards a single or a weighted sum of reward functions. Several methods (Paulus et al., 2018;Çelikyilmaz et al., 2018) adopt the ROUGE-L score (Lin, 2004) as the reward function. The SENECA model (Sharma et al., 2019) optimizes a weighted sum of ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, and a coherence score from a coherence model. To improve the factual correctness of the generated summaries, several methods (Huang et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020c) use RL to maximize a weighted sum of ROUGE scores and a factual correctness score computed by a model. Kryscinski et al. (2018) use the weighted sum of ROUGE-L and 3-gram novelty as the reward to increase the abstractiveness of summaries, but this method does not allow users to control the abstractiveness level of summaries. Pasunuru and Bansal (2018) extend the ROUGE-L reward by up-weighting the salient words detected by a classifier.

documents.snippet:
Abstractive summarization. Most of the existing abstractive summarization models (Gehrmann et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020a;Chan et al., 2020) are built on the encoder-decoder model (Bahdanau et al., 2015) to generate summaries. See et al. (2017) propose the pointer-generator network which allows copying words from the source to the output summary. The structure-infused copy mechanism (Song et al., 2018) incorporates the syntactic structure of the source text into the pointer-generator network to facilitate copying important words to the output summary. Lebanoff et al. (2019) propose a summarization framework that first extracts either a single sentence or a pair of sentences from the source document, then it condenses or fuses the selected sentence(s) to generate a summary. The above models do not allow users to constrain the degree of copying nor sentence fusion from the source document. 

Recent methods apply RL with MDP to optimize an abstractive summarization model towards a single or a weighted sum of reward functions. Several methods (Paulus et al., 2018;Çelikyilmaz et al., 2018) adopt the ROUGE-L score (Lin, 2004) as the reward function. The SENECA model (Sharma et al., 2019) optimizes a weighted sum of ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, and a coherence score from a coherence model. To improve the factual correctness of the generated summaries, several methods (Huang et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020c) use RL to maximize a weighted sum of ROUGE scores and a factual correctness score computed by a model. Kryscinski et al. (2018) use the weighted sum of ROUGE-L and 3-gram novelty as the reward to increase the abstractiveness of summaries, but this method does not allow users to control the abstractiveness level of summaries. Pasunuru and Bansal (2018) extend the ROUGE-L reward by up-weighting the salient words detected by a classifier.

Further, our method allows for control over copying during both training and decoding stages of the neural model. We experiment with varying proportions of seen and unseen summary words in training to teach the summarizer to favor, or not to favor, copying. At decoding time, we compare different search strategies (bestfirst search vs. beam search) and reranking methods to encourage system abstracts to use wording similar to the original. Despite that only single reference summaries are available in benchmark evaluations, we are able to evaluate summary quality along multiple dimensions, using automatic metrics based on lexical similarity (ROUGE; Lin, 2004) and semantic similarity (BERTScore; Zhang et al., 2019), and through human assessment of grammaticality, informativeness, and whether system abstracts remain true-to-original. Such summaries are highly desirable to cater to diverse real-world scenarios; 1 • our method emphasizes on in-depth analysis of the copy behavior in summarization. Title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: The main focus of this work is not to propose a solution to hallucination related issues, but to achieve a better understanding of hallucinations in abstractive summarization through their human assessment. We randomly sampled 500 articles from the test set to facilitate our study. Using the full test set was unfeasible given its size and the cost of human judgments. We have trained annotators (fluent in English) specifically for our assessment. Our annotators went through two pilot studies to have a better understanding of intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations, and factuality of summaries. Documents used in the pilot studies were not used in the final annotation. We also report on ROUGE (Lin and Hovy, 2003) scores, BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020) and semantic inference metric such as textual entailment (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018;Welleck et al., 2019;Falke et al., 2019;Kryscinski et al., 2019b) and question answering (Arumae and Liu, 2019;Wang et al., 2020). (Lin and Hovy, 2003) provides a means to quickly assess a model's ability to generate summaries closer to human authored summaries. We report on ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 for informativeness and ROUGE-L, for fluency. Like ROUGE, BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020) computes a similarity score for each token in the candidate sum- mary with each token in the reference summary. However, instead of exact matches, it computes token similarity using contextual embeddings. Results are presented in Table 1.

Title: All for law and law for all: Adaptive RAG Pipeline for Legal Research
Snippet: Our initial setup included ROUGE recall (average of ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L) as one of the core metrics to evaluate content overlap with reference answers. However, as shown in Figure 4, we observe that ROUGE recall exhibits a declining trend as the number of retrieved chunks (k) increases, in contrast to metrics such as BERTScore F1 and RAGA Faithfulness/Relevancy, which stabilise or improve. This discrepancy motivated an in-depth investigation of the limitations of ROUGE in this context. 

ROUGE was originally designed to evaluate extractive summarization by computing n-gram overlap between generated and reference texts (Chalkidis et al., 2020). While effective for summarisation and simple question-answering scenarios, it falls short in evaluating abstractive or semantically equivalent generation, especially when the wording differs from the reference but the meaning is preserved. Hence, for more meaningful and context-aware evaluation, we focus on RAGAS Faithfulness and Relevancy, which accounts for whether the answer is grounded in retrieved content; BERTScore F1 (Exploding Gradients, 2025), which reflects semantic similarity at the embedding level. By excluding ROUGE recall, we avoid penalising correct responses that diverge lexically, and better align our evaluation metrics with the goals of faithful and relevant generation.

Title: Reducing Hallucinations in Summarization via Reinforcement Learning with Entity Hallucination Index
Snippet: Abstractive summarization models, powered by large language models (LLMs), have achieved impressive results across various domains. However, a persistent challenge remains: hallucination, where generated summaries include incorrect or fabricated information not grounded in the source input (Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020). In high-stakes applications such as meeting summarization, medical reporting, or financial documentation, hallucinations, particularly involving named entities, can significantly undermine trustworthiness and utility. 

Existing work on hallucination detection primarily focuses on coarse-grained factuality metrics or relies on reference-based evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Pagnoni et al., 2021). While such methods are valuable, they often fail to capture fine-grained entity-level hallucinations, and their dependence on ground-truth references limits scalability. Recent efforts have explored lightweight automatic metrics, yet integrating such evaluations directly into model training remains underexplored. 

In this work, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach that leverages the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI) as a reward signal to reduce hallucinations at the entity level. EHI quantifies the correctness and grounding of entities by comparing extracted entities from model outputs to those present in the input document, enabling efficient evaluation with reduced reference. We first generate baseline summaries using a pre-trained model, compute EHI scores through automatic entity extraction and matching, and fine-tune the model using reinforcement learning with EHI as the reward function. This method biases the model toward producing more entity-faithful summaries without requiring human factuality annotations. 

Our contributions are as follows: 

• We introduce an EHI-guided fine-tuning framework that improves entity faithfulness in abstractive summarization. 

• We present a scalable reinforcement learning pipeline that does not depend on humanlabeled factuality datasets. 

• We demonstrate empirical improvements in EHI scores across meeting transcript datasets and conduct qualitative analysis to highlight reductions in hallucination. 

• We release a reproducible Colab-based implementation to facilitate further research on hallucination-aware summarization.

Title: Abstractive text summarization: State of the art, challenges, and improvements
Snippet: Jang et al. [97] addressed the limitations of traditional ROUGE-L based methods, which often generate repetitive summaries, by introducing two new RL reward functions: ROUGE-SIM and ROUGE-WMD. These functions integrate Cosine Similarity and Word Mover's Distance [106] respectively, with the ROUGE-L score, ensuring summaries are semantically close to the source text while promoting novelty and reducing direct copying. To generate accurate, innovative, and grammatically sound summaries, a decoding method based on these reward functions was proposed. The Gigaword dataset was employed to evaluate the new methods. The authors used three metrics: ROUGE-PACKAGE, novel n-grams, and Grammarly9 to measure summary quality, originality, and grammatical integrity. The proposed models surpassed various baselines, offering consistent performance, higher semantic value, improved abstractiveness, and reduced grammatical errors. 

Keneshloo et al. [98] introduced an RL framework for abstractive text summarization to address exposure bias and improve generalization to unfamiliar datasets. Exposure bias means that during the training phase, the model is provided with an accurate input at every decoder step, while in the testing phase, it must generate the next token based on its own output [98]. They used a Pointer-Generator [41] model combined with an RL objective and a transfer reinforcement learning approach. Traditional methods relying on cross-entropy (CE) loss often suffer from exposure bias and poor generalization. In contrast, the proposed RL objective minimizes the negative expected reward, enabling the model to train based on its own output, in line with metrics like ROUGE. This self-critical policy gradient approach emphasizes better-performing samples during training. However, the model faced challenges in transfer learning due to training on the source dataset distribution. To counter this, they introduced a transfer RL approach using a shared encoder and a trade-off parameter to balance source and target dataset training. The authors used four datasets: Newsroom [107], CNN/Daily Mail, DUC 2003 10 , and DUC 2004 11 , for training and evaluating text summarization models. They evaluated the models using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F1 scores.

snippet.text:
Abstractive summarization models, powered by large language models (LLMs), have achieved impressive results across various domains. However, a persistent challenge remains: hallucination, where generated summaries include incorrect or fabricated information not grounded in the source input (Maynez et al., 2020;Durmus et al., 2020). In high-stakes applications such as meeting summarization, medical reporting, or financial documentation, hallucinations, particularly involving named entities, can significantly undermine trustworthiness and utility. 

Existing work on hallucination detection primarily focuses on coarse-grained factuality metrics or relies on reference-based evaluations (Falke et al., 2019;Pagnoni et al., 2021). While such methods are valuable, they often fail to capture fine-grained entity-level hallucinations, and their dependence on ground-truth references limits scalability. Recent efforts have explored lightweight automatic metrics, yet integrating such evaluations directly into model training remains underexplored. 

In this work, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach that leverages the Entity Hallucination Index (EHI) as a reward signal to reduce hallucinations at the entity level. EHI quantifies the correctness and grounding of entities by comparing extracted entities from model outputs to those present in the input document, enabling efficient evaluation with reduced reference. We first generate baseline summaries using a pre-trained model, compute EHI scores through automatic entity extraction and matching, and fine-tune the model using reinforcement learning with EHI as the reward function. This method biases the model toward producing more entity-faithful summaries without requiring human factuality annotations. 

Our contributions are as follows: 

• We introduce an EHI-guided fine-tuning framework that improves entity faithfulness in abstractive summarization. 

• We present a scalable reinforcement learning pipeline that does not depend on humanlabeled factuality datasets. 

• We demonstrate empirical improvements in EHI scores across meeting transcript datasets and conduct qualitative analysis to highlight reductions in hallucination. 

• We release a reproducible Colab-based implementation to facilitate further research on hallucination-aware summarization.

snippet.text:
Jang et al. [97] addressed the limitations of traditional ROUGE-L based methods, which often generate repetitive summaries, by introducing two new RL reward functions: ROUGE-SIM and ROUGE-WMD. These functions integrate Cosine Similarity and Word Mover's Distance [106] respectively, with the ROUGE-L score, ensuring summaries are semantically close to the source text while promoting novelty and reducing direct copying. To generate accurate, innovative, and grammatically sound summaries, a decoding method based on these reward functions was proposed. The Gigaword dataset was employed to evaluate the new methods. The authors used three metrics: ROUGE-PACKAGE, novel n-grams, and Grammarly9 to measure summary quality, originality, and grammatical integrity. The proposed models surpassed various baselines, offering consistent performance, higher semantic value, improved abstractiveness, and reduced grammatical errors. 

Keneshloo et al. [98] introduced an RL framework for abstractive text summarization to address exposure bias and improve generalization to unfamiliar datasets. Exposure bias means that during the training phase, the model is provided with an accurate input at every decoder step, while in the testing phase, it must generate the next token based on its own output [98]. They used a Pointer-Generator [41] model combined with an RL objective and a transfer reinforcement learning approach. Traditional methods relying on cross-entropy (CE) loss often suffer from exposure bias and poor generalization. In contrast, the proposed RL objective minimizes the negative expected reward, enabling the model to train based on its own output, in line with metrics like ROUGE. This self-critical policy gradient approach emphasizes better-performing samples during training. However, the model faced challenges in transfer learning due to training on the source dataset distribution. To counter this, they introduced a transfer RL approach using a shared encoder and a trade-off parameter to balance source and target dataset training. The authors used four datasets: Newsroom [107], CNN/Daily Mail, DUC 2003 10 , and DUC 2004 11 , for training and evaluating text summarization models. They evaluated the models using ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F1 scores.

Such summaries are highly desirable to cater to diverse real-world scenarios; 1 • our method emphasizes on in-depth analysis of the copy behavior in summarization. It frames abstractive summarization as a language modeling task and exploits multiple strategies at training and decoding stages to generate diverse summary hypotheses. We show competitive results and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on exercising control over copying.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of how training-data interventions can prevent hallucinations in abstractive summarization when intrinsic (faithfulness/factuality) and extrinsic (coverage/ROUGE-like) metrics disagree on what counts as an error. I first summarize the disagreement, then explain mechanisms and concrete interventions, and finally tie them to outcomes.

1) Why hallucinations and their metrics disagree in summarization
- In abstractive summarization, hallucinations are often split into intrinsic (contradictions or misrepresentations within the source) and extrinsic (adding content not supported by the source or world knowledge). These categories are conceptually distinct but hard to separate automatically, and much current work uses model-based or unsupervised proxies that conflate them or rely on semi-supervised signals like QA-based consistency checks <cite id="30249a55-0">Existing hallucination metrics for abstractive summarization are mainly model-based and unsupervised; it is difficult to automatically distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic hallucinations</cite> <cite id="30249a55-1">An abstract summary is hallucinated if it contains spans not semantically supported by the input; intrinsic hallucinations are contradictions with the input (e.g., wrong pronouns, swapped names/verbs), while extrinsic hallucinations are unsupported spans; models can overfit to extrinsic hallucinations present in training summaries</cite>.
- Extrinsic metrics like ROUGE measure lexical/sequence overlap and often fail to capture semantic faithfulness; empirical and survey evidence shows poor correlation with human judgments on hallucinations and other factuality properties. This means ROUGE can reward fluent, long, or extractive summaries that contain unsupported claims or distortions <cite id="29b9d831-0">Similarity metrics like ROUGE often fail to measure faithfulness; intrinsic vs extrinsic hallucinations cannot be discerned by a single number; ROUGE-like metrics frequently misalign with human factuality annotations</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-1">SOTA abstractive summarization systems evaluated with ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR still hallucinate; traditional metrics have poor correlation with human judgment on hallucination; FRANK and TRUE assess faithfulness metrics and their correlation with human judgments</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-2">QAFactEval measures factual consistency of summary–source pairs via QA but is biased toward extractive summaries</cite>.
- The disagreement has real consequences: models trained to maximize extrinsic overlap can inherit and amplify extrinsic hallucinations from training data, and human annotators often tolerate certain extrinsic inferences in domains like clinical narratives, further straining metric alignment <cite id="30249a55-1">Sequence-to-sequence models can amplify extrinsic hallucinations present in human-written summaries during training</cite> <cite id="30249a55-4">In clinical discharge summarization, intrinsic hallucination misrepresents stated facts, while extrinsic hallucination adds content not stated but possibly inferable by experts; some extrinsic additions may not be considered hallucinations in this domain even though other work defines hallucinations more rigidly</cite>.

2) Mechanisms: how training-data interventions target the sources of hallucination
- Data selection and cleaning to steer away from noisy in-context exemplars. If model behavior is sensitive to noisy or hallucinated training samples, selecting “clean” subsets by faithfulness and fine-tuning—while contrasting against “noisy” subsets—can shift parameters toward faithful generalization. This aligns training signals with intrinsic faithfulness rather than extrinsic overlap and can improve factual metrics and human eval without hurting informativeness <cite id="30249a55-3">Hallucination degree may depend on errors in training data; CaPE selects clean/noisy subsets by automatic factual metrics, fine-tunes expert/anti-expert models, and adjusts base parameters toward the expert, improving summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy on XSUM and CNN/DM by up to 16.69% and 15.78% while maintaining informativeness (ROUGE)</cite>.
- Faithfulness-constrained objectives and QA-grounded supervision. Training objectives that penalize unsupported claims (e.g., via QA-style evidence retrieval for each claim, consistency checks, or entailment) make generation accountable to the source and world knowledge, reducing intrinsic hallucinations while preserving coverage. Metrics like QAFactEval operationalize such supervision by converting each summarized fact into verifiable QA pairs and measuring consistency against the source; this directly addresses intrinsic errors even when ROUGE remains high <cite id="29b9d831-2">QAFactEval turns each named entity in a summary into questions, answers them against the source with QA metrics (EM, F1, LERC), and measures consistency—effectively enforcing evidence links that reduce unsupported content</cite> <cite id="30249a55-2">Reducing hallucinations in summarization entails increasing faithfulness and factual consistency between source and summary; early correction of hallucinated content is crucial due to the “snowball effect” where inaccuracies propagate</cite>.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Hallucination is a known issue for neural abstractive summarization models. Recent work suggests that the degree of hallucination may depend on errors in the training data. In this work, we propose a new method called Contrastive Parameter Ensembling (CaPE) to use training data more effectively, utilizing variations in noise in training samples to reduce hallucination. We first select clean and noisy subsets from the training data using different automatic factual metrics. Then, we fine-tune a base summarization model, which is trained on all training samples, on the clean (noisy) subset to obtain an \textit{expert} (\textit{anti-expert}) model. Finally, we adjust the parameters of base model by the difference between parameters of the \textit{expert} and \textit{anti-expert} models, steering the base model towards the \textit{expert} model and away from the \textit{anti-expert} model. Experimental results show that CaPE improves performance across different automatic factual metrics and human evaluation, with the maximum improvement of 16.69\% and 15.78\% on summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy for the XSUM and CNN/DM datasets. The improvement in factual performance does not degrade the performance on other metrics of informativeness such as ROUGE.

Title: Repairing the Cracked Foundation: A Survey of Obstacles in Evaluation Practices for Generated Text
Snippet: An aspect of quality mentioned above and which permeates all of NLG is faithfulness, and much recent work has focused on this aspect for abstractive summarization. Maynez et al. (2020) state that a model is not faithful if it hallucinates, that is, it adds information that is not present in the source document. They define multiple categories of hallucinations: Intrinsic hallucinations misrepresent facts in the input, for example turning a "former London mayoral candidate" into a "former London mayor". Extrinsic hallucinations ignore the input altogether, for example generating "President Sara" in the example above. Not all hallucinations are problematic-an extrinsic hallucination can be factual, and may, in fact, be desirable depending on the use case. For system evaluation, it is therefore important to be able to discern between hallucinations of different types, which cannot be done by producing a single number. 

Maynez et al. demonstrate that similarity metrics fail to measure faithfulness. The same failure is observed by Pagnoni et al. (2021) who introduce and collect annotations for an alternative typology of factual errors which involves fine-grained categories such as Coreference Error and Out of Article Error. In an alternative approach to measuring correlations with human judgments, Gabriel et al. (2021) inject factual errors in reference summaries, and checks whether system rankings produced by metrics correlate with the "level of factuality" of the transformed sentences, among other properties like a metric's value range and generalization. They also identify that standard evaluation metrics (e.g., ROUGE-L and ROUGE-1) oftentimes fail at capturing factuality, but identify questionanswering metrics as promising, somewhat contradicting Maynez et al.. Similarly, Chen et al. (2021) analyze mispredictions on a set of previously annotated summarization corpora (Kryscinski et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020;Falke et al., 2019;Maynez et al., 2020).
</snippet>

Title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
Snippet: Recently, various studies have illustrated that most conventional metrics used to measure the quality of writing are not adequate for quantifying the level of hallucination [22,26]. It has been shown that State-of-the-Art (SOTA) abstractive summarization systems, evaluated with metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR, have hallucinated content in 25% of their generated summaries [32]. A similar phenomenon has been shown in other NLG tasks, where it has been discovered that traditional metrics have a poor correlation with human judgment in terms of the hallucination problem [22,26,54,66]. Therefore, there are active research efforts to define effective metrics for quantifying hallucination, as summarized in Table 2. FRANK [99] surveys the faithfulness metrics for summarization and compares these metrics' correlations with human judgments. To assess the example-level accuracy of metrics in diverse tasks, TRUE [53] reports their area under the ROC curve (ROC AUC) in regard to hallucinated example detection.
</snippet>

Title: BRIDO: Bringing Democratic Order to Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We choose the metrics to cover the various summarization and hallucination metrics. 

ROUGE Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (Lin 2004) measures the lexical similarity between summaries and human-written references by comparing the overlap of n-grams, which are sequences of n words. The most common variants of ROUGE include ROUGE-N (for n-gram matching) and ROUGE-L (for longest common subsequence matching). Among these, we use ROUGE-1 (R-1), ROUGE-2 (R-2), and ROUGE-L (R-L) for evaluation. For the ranking, we use 2 R-1 × R-2/(R-1 + R-2) for XSum and (R-1 + R-2 + R-L)/3 for CNN/DM following Liu et al. (2022a). ROUGE's limitation includes the lexical bias and the questionable quality of the reference. In this work, we generalize this conventional definition of ROUGE and use it to measure the lexical similarity between summary candidates as well. 

QAFactEval (Fabbri et al. 2022) is a QA-Based Factual Consistency Evaluation without a reference. Given a summary and the source document, it uses a question generation model to generate questions for each of the named entities. It then uses the source document as a reference for the question-answering model to generate the answers for each question. It evaluates the answers with the true answer and measures the consistency of a summary with its source document. The submetrics (LERC, F1, EM, and IsAns) are the methods used in comparing the model answer with the true answer. LERC has a maximum score of 5 and F1, EM, and IsAns are measured in percent. QAFactEval, like all other QA-based factuality metrics, suffers from bias towards extractive summaries. (Liu et al. 2023b) is a framework for using large language models with chain-of-thoughts (CoT) and a formfilling paradigm to assess the quality of NLG outputs. G-Eval consists of four sub-metrics which are coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance.
</snippet>

Title: HaRiM^+: Evaluating Summary Quality with Hallucination Risk
Snippet: Although recent state-of-the-art summarization models have achieved remarkable performances (Lewis et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020), appropriate metrics for measuring faithfulness of the generated summaries are still needed. The practice of measuring performance in the summarization task heavily relies on the N-gram matching based metric, ROUGE (Lin, 2004). Reportedly, ROUGE barely satisfies more than indicating lexical similarity (Maynez et al., 2020) and does not consider semantic dimensions of the generation, which current research needs of. 

There have been numerous attempts to come up with faithfulness evaluation metrics (Novikova et al., 2017;Peyrard, 2019). Neural-based metrics have demonstrated good performances in estimating the factual consistency of a summaryarticle pair with semantic entailment (Kryscinski et al., 2020;Goyal and Durrett, 2020), questionanswering framework (Wang et al., 2020;Scialom et al., 2021Scialom et al., , 2019)), and text generation (Yuan et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2021). Most of the model-asa-metric approach generally requires fine-tuning or complicated pipelines. Consequently, evaluating generated texts with recent model-as-a-metric methods has become cumbersome. 

With the increased demand for faithful generation models, it has come to a lot of attention on reformulating training objectives for purported for this (Zhang et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2022a;Holtzman et al., 2018). We focus on the training objective suggested in (Miao et al., 2021), which directly targets hallucination problems in generating sentences given a source context. Miao et al. suggest that an overconfident decoder causes hallucination since the model excessively pays attention to the previously generated tokens over the source context which is in line with (Bowman et al., 2016).
</snippet>
<snippet id=29b9d831-4>
Title: A Graph-theoretic Summary Evaluation for ROUGE
Snippet: We evaluate ROUGE-G, against the top metrics (C S IIITH3, DemokritosGR1, Catolicasc1) among the 23 metrics participated in TAC AESOP 2011, ROUGE, and the most recent related work (ROUGE-WE) (Table 1). Overall results support our proposal to consider semantics besides surface with ROUGE. Since the large/small differences in competing correlations with human assessment are not an acceptable proof of superiority/inferiority in performance of one metric over another, significance tests should be applied. To better clarify the effectiveness of ROUGE-G, we have used pairwise Williams significance test recommended by Graham et al. (2015) for summarization evaluation. Accordingly, evaluation of a given summarization metric, M new , takes the form of quantifying three correlations: r(M new , H), that exists between the evaluation metric scores for summarization systems and corresponding human assessment scores; r(M base , H), that stands for the correlation of baseline metrics with human judges; and the third correlation, between evaluation metric scores themselves, r(M base , M new ). It can happen for a pair of competing metrics for which the correlation between metric scores is strong, that a small difference in competing correlations with human assessment is significant, while, for a different pair of metrics with a larger difference in correlation, the difference is not significant (Graham et al., 2015). Using this significance test, the results show that all increases in correlations of ROUGE-G compared to ROUGE and ROUGE-WE variants are statistically significant (p < 0.05). We analyze the correlation results reported in Table 1 in the following. ROUGE-G-2 achieves the best correlation with Pyramid, regarding all correlation metrics. Moreover, every ROUGE-G variant outperforms its corresponding ROUGE and ROUGE-WE variants, regardless of the correlation metric used. However, the only exception is ROUGE-SU4, which correlates slightly better with Pyramid when measuring with Pearson correlation. One possible reason is that Pyramid measures content similarity between peer and model summaries, while the variants of ROUGE-G favor semantics behind the content for measuring similarities.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: Self-Consistency as a Free Lunch: Reducing Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Self-Reflection
Snippet: To address uncertainty and over-reliance on biased patterns in training data, several works focus on detecting hallucinations with external feedback within its outputs. First type of feedback is through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [24] to guide the models respond based on visual-grounded cues. Silkie [33] utilizes the powerful GPT-4V [4] to generate feedback to help it generate visually faithful responses. A recent method RLAIF-V [16] incorporate a divide-and-conquer strategy, where responses are split into atomic claims, allowing models to evaluate the validity of each component. This approach assesses the validity of each claim using either an external powerful VLM or the original model with binary questions. Then the responses are rated using the produced validity scores and used to generate training pairs for Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) [34]. This approach relies on peer feedback-using other opensource MLLMs as the feedback source. While it avoids dependence on powerful external superior models used in superior-teacher methods, it still requires additional models and cannot reduce hallucinations on its own. In contrast to existing work, we focus on harvesting feedback from the target model itself, which does not require expansive human annotation or powerful external models.
</snippet>
<snippet id=26850444-1>
Title: Volcano: Mitigating Multimodal Hallucination through Self-Feedback Guided Revision
Snippet: Previous methods for mitigating multimodal hallucinations have varied in their focus, including enhancing the quality of instruction tuning data, model training methodologies, and implementing post-hoc refinements. LRV-Instruction dataset (Liu et al., 2023a) ensures the balance of both negative and positive instructions and VIGC (Wang et al., 2023a) iteratively generates and corrects instructions to reduce hallucinated samples in training data. Adapting reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to train a single reward model as in LLaVA-RLHF (Sun et al., 2023) or training multiple or even without no reward models as in FDPO (Gunjal et al., 2023) has proven effective as well. LURE (Zhou et al., 2023) trains a revision model to detect and correct hallucinated objects in the base model's response. Woodpecker (Yin et al., 2023) breaks down the revision process into multiple subtasks where three pre-trained models apart from the base LMM are employed for the subtasks. 

Unlike models using reinforcement learning, our approach does not require reward model training. Also, contrary to revision-only methods, our method trains a model to self -revise, eliminating the need for extra modules. Furthermore, we introduce natural language feedback before the revision process. This feedback serves a dual purpose: it revisits the visual features for enhanced clarity and specifically pinpoints the hallucinated elements that require correction, thereby enriching the information available for more effective revision.
</snippet>

Title: AI-Powered Annotation Pipelines for Stabilizing Large Language Models: A Human-AI Synergy Approach

Nonetheless, problems of RLHF are a lack of generalisability and the presence of few, high-quality annotated feedbacks, particularly when model capabilities are increased (Dong et al., 2023). 

Things that can be included are complementary methods:

Title: Rewarding Intellectual Humility Learning When Not To Answer In Large Language Models
Snippet: Alignment methods such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) have been shown to reduce hallucinations but not eliminate them. (Ouyang et al., 2022) introduced SFT followed by RLHF using human demonstrations, while (Bai et al., 2022) optimized preference models to balance helpfulness and harmlessness; both approaches rely on costly human feedback and do not explicitly model uncertainty. (Lambert et al., 2025) surveyed these methods, identifying hallucination as a persistent failure mode and motivating the need for more verifiable reward structures. 

More closely related, (Godin et al., 2019) proposed a ternary reward structure that explicitly rewards abstention in question answering, improving precision and reducing hallucinations. However, this work predates modern instruction-tuned LLMs and does not study abstention within contemporary SFT or RL-based training pipelines. In contrast, our work integrates abstention-aware supervision into modern LLM alignment and evaluation, enabling calibrated refusal behavior without relying solely on dense human preference feedback.
</snippet>

Title: RLAIF-V: Open-Source AI Feedback Leads to Super GPT-4V Trustworthiness
Snippet: Traditional feedback learning for hallucination reduction relies on labor-intensive manual labeling or expensive proprietary models. This leaves the community without foundational knowledge about how to build high-quality feedback with open-source MLLMs. In this work, we introduce RLAIF-V, a novel framework that aligns MLLMs in a fully open-source paradigm. RLAIF-V maximally explores open-source MLLMs from two perspectives, including high-quality feedback data generation for preference learning and self-feedback guidance for inference-time scaling. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks in both automatic and human evaluation show that RLAIF-V substantially enhances the trustworthiness of models at both preference learning and inference time. RLAIF-V 7B reduces object hallucination by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7%. Remarkably, RLAIF-V 12B further reveals the self-alignment potential of open-source MLLMs, where the model can learn from feedback of itself to achieve super GPT-4V trustworthiness.
