Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of how training-data interventions can prevent hallucinations in abstractive summarization when intrinsic (faithfulness/factuality) and extrinsic (coverage/ROUGE-like) metrics disagree on what counts as an error. I first summarize the disagreement, then explain mechanisms and concrete interventions, and finally tie them to outcomes.

1) Why hallucinations and their metrics disagree in summarization
- In abstractive summarization, hallucinations are often split into intrinsic (contradictions or misrepresentations within the source) and extrinsic (adding content not supported by the source or world knowledge). These categories are conceptually distinct but hard to separate automatically, and much current work uses model-based or unsupervised proxies that conflate them or rely on semi-supervised signals like QA-based consistency checks <cite id="30249a55-0">Existing hallucination metrics for abstractive summarization are mainly model-based and unsupervised; it is difficult to automatically distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic hallucinations</cite> <cite id="30249a55-1">An abstract summary is hallucinated if it contains spans not semantically supported by the input; intrinsic hallucinations are contradictions with the input (e.g., wrong pronouns, swapped names/verbs), while extrinsic hallucinations are unsupported spans; models can overfit to extrinsic hallucinations present in training summaries</cite>.
- Extrinsic metrics like ROUGE measure lexical/sequence overlap and often fail to capture semantic faithfulness; empirical and survey evidence shows poor correlation with human judgments on hallucinations and other factuality properties. This means ROUGE can reward fluent, long, or extractive summaries that contain unsupported claims or distortions <cite id="29b9d831-0">Similarity metrics like ROUGE often fail to measure faithfulness; intrinsic vs extrinsic hallucinations cannot be discerned by a single number; ROUGE-like metrics frequently misalign with human factuality annotations</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-1">SOTA abstractive summarization systems evaluated with ROUGE/BLEU/METEOR still hallucinate; traditional metrics have poor correlation with human judgment on hallucination; FRANK and TRUE assess faithfulness metrics and their correlation with human judgments</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-2">QAFactEval measures factual consistency of summary–source pairs via QA but is biased toward extractive summaries</cite>.
- The disagreement has real consequences: models trained to maximize extrinsic overlap can inherit and amplify extrinsic hallucinations from training data, and human annotators often tolerate certain extrinsic inferences in domains like clinical narratives, further straining metric alignment <cite id="30249a55-1">Sequence-to-sequence models can amplify extrinsic hallucinations present in human-written summaries during training</cite> <cite id="30249a55-4">In clinical discharge summarization, intrinsic hallucination misrepresents stated facts, while extrinsic hallucination adds content not stated but possibly inferable by experts; some extrinsic additions may not be considered hallucinations in this domain even though other work defines hallucinations more rigidly</cite>.

2) Mechanisms: how training-data interventions target the sources of hallucination
- Data selection and cleaning to steer away from noisy in-context exemplars. If model behavior is sensitive to noisy or hallucinated training samples, selecting “clean” subsets by faithfulness and fine-tuning—while contrasting against “noisy” subsets—can shift parameters toward faithful generalization. This aligns training signals with intrinsic faithfulness rather than extrinsic overlap and can improve factual metrics and human eval without hurting informativeness <cite id="30249a55-3">Hallucination degree may depend on errors in training data; CaPE selects clean/noisy subsets by automatic factual metrics, fine-tunes expert/anti-expert models, and adjusts base parameters toward the expert, improving summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy on XSUM and CNN/DM by up to 16.69% and 15.78% while maintaining informativeness (ROUGE)</cite>.
- Faithfulness-constrained objectives and QA-grounded supervision. Training objectives that penalize unsupported claims (e.g., via QA-style evidence retrieval for each claim, consistency checks, or entailment) make generation accountable to the source and world knowledge, reducing intrinsic hallucinations while preserving coverage. Metrics like QAFactEval operationalize such supervision by converting each summarized fact into verifiable QA pairs and measuring consistency against the source; this directly addresses intrinsic errors even when ROUGE remains high <cite id="29b9d831-2">QAFactEval turns each named entity in a summary into questions, answers them against the source with QA metrics (EM, F1, LERC), and measures consistency—effectively enforcing evidence links that reduce unsupported content</cite> <cite id="30249a55-2">Reducing hallucinations in summarization entails increasing faithfulness and factual consistency between source and summary; early correction of hallucinated content is crucial due to the “snowball effect” where inaccuracies propagate</cite>.
- Evidence-grounded generation and early error correction. Interventions that require explicit evidence linking claims to the source (e.g., evidence retrieval per sentence, constrained templates, or chain-of-thought with verification) reduce intrinsic hallucinations at generation time. Training on faithfulness-oriented corpora and using model-as-a-metric ensembles can catch contradictions early, mitigating the compounding of errors that intrinsic content tends to trigger <cite id="30249a55-2">Intrinsic hallucinations contradict the input; extrinsic hallucinations ignore the input; early correction is crucial because initial inaccuracies tend to propagate in abstractive chains</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-0">Model-as-a-metric approaches (e.g., entailment, QA-based factuality) can detect factual errors across categories; intrinsic vs extrinsic cannot be captured by single-number metrics, motivating multi-metric training signals</cite>.
- Model-as-a-metric and AI/peer-feedback alignment. When extrinsic metrics mislead, training on feedback from stronger evaluators (human or AI) or preference learning can align generation with faithful output. Methods that decompose responses into atomic claims, rate claim validity, and use these as supervision (e.g., RLAIF-V) reduce hallucination rates substantially, including object hallucinations and overall hallucinations, and extend to inference-time self-feedback—closing the loop between evaluation and training <cite id="26850444-0">RLHF and AI-feedback methods (e.g., RLAIF-V) evaluate claim validity via external models or binary questions, use validity scores to produce training pairs, and guide models toward visually faithful responses</cite> <cite id="26850444-4">RLAIF-V uses self-generated feedback to train preference policies; on six benchmarks, it reduces object hallucination by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7%, improving both automatic and human evaluations</cite>.
- Instruction/data curation tailored to hallucination risk. Curating instruction sets that include balanced positive and negative examples, and iteratively generating/correcting instruction data to remove hallucinated samples, improves instruction-tuned baselines’ factualization and reduces overconfident, unsupported claims. This combats the “snowball effect” by conditioning models on corrected exemplars that explicitly reject unsupported inferences <cite id="26850444-1">The LRV-Instruction dataset balances negative and positive instructions; VIGC iteratively generates and corrects instructions to reduce hallucinated training samples; adapting RLHF and training without reward models have shown effectiveness as complementary methods</cite> <cite id="30249a55-2">Overconfident decoding causes hallucination by over-attending to previously generated tokens over the source; interventions that enforce early source attention and correction reduce cascading errors</cite>.

3) Bridging the intrinsic–extrinsic gap with training-data interventions and outcomes
- Multi-metric training signals that privilege intrinsic faithfulness while preserving extrinsic quality. Contrastive parameter ensembling demonstrates that selecting clean vs noisy subsets by factual metrics and fine-tuning accordingly improves dependency-arc entailment and other factuality measures by double-digit percentages, without degrading ROUGE—indicating that training-data interventions can reduce hallucinations while maintaining coverage and fluency <cite id="30249a55-3">CaPE improves summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy on XSUM and CNN/DM by up to 16.69% and 15.78%, and the factual performance gains do not harm informativeness metrics like ROUGE</cite>.
- Data-centric evaluation loops: filtering by factuality and retraining. Because ROUGE is lexical and can miss factual errors, iterative filtering of training data by factuality metrics and retraining reduces intrinsic hallucinations. Surveys and studies show that QA-based and entailment-based metrics are better at detecting factual inconsistencies than ROUGE; integrating these into data selection yields summaries that humans judge as more faithful, even if ROUGE improves modestly or plateaus <cite id="29b9d831-0">Standard similarity metrics often fail to capture factuality; QA-based and entailment approaches better detect factual errors across intrinsic/extrinsic types, necessitating multi-metric evaluation and training</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-1">FRANK and TRUE show many faithfulness metrics correlate differently with human judgments; using such metrics to filter training data can reduce hallucinations better aligned with human faithfulness</cite>.
- Alignment via AI feedback reduces absolute hallucination rates and improves human assessments. Even when ROUGE remains a poor proxy, RL/RLAIF-style feedback targeting claim-level validity yields large reductions in hallucinations and improves human evaluations, indicating that training-data interventions grounded in stronger evaluators can overcome metric misalignment <cite id="26850444-4">RLAIF-V substantially enhances trustworthiness; object hallucination drops by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7%, with gains on both automatic and human evaluations</cite> <cite id="26850444-0">RLHF and RLAIF-V leverage external or self-generated feedback to validate claims and adjust training data/policies toward visually faithful outputs</cite>.
- Domain-specific calibration and guardrails. In domains like clinical narratives, some extrinsic inferences are acceptable; training-data interventions can incorporate domain-specific rules (e.g., citeable inference boundaries) and QA against clinical sources to distinguish benign inference from unsupported hallucination, aligning models with expert tolerance while enforcing minimum evidence standards <cite id="30249a55-4">Complementary statements not explicitly stated in inpatient records may be inferred by medical professionals and not considered hallucinations in discharge summaries, whereas other work defines hallucinations more strictly; this underscores the need for domain-tailored definitions and training data</cite>.

- When ROUGE is high but human faithfulness is low, suspect intrinsic hallucinations. Use QA-based factuality (QAFactEval), entailment, or FRANK-style fine-grained error typing to identify intrinsic errors, then apply data interventions: filter out high-ROUGE/low-factuality summaries from training, add evidence-linking objectives, and retrain. Expect improvements on entailment/consistency and human faithfulness without necessarily improving ROUGE, as coverage is preserved but unsupported content is penalized <cite id="29b9d831-2">QAFactEval operationalizes source-grounded consistency checks that penalize unsupported content, counteracting extractive biases</cite> <cite id="30249a55-3">CaPE shows that clean/noisy subset contrastive fine-tuning can raise factuality metrics substantially while keeping ROUGE stable</cite>.
- When training data contain extrinsic hallucinations, models will amplify them. Curate and de-hallucinate training corpora by automated filtering plus targeted human checks, and add instruction/data augmentations that explicitly reject unsupported claims. This addresses the “snowball effect” and stabilizes generation toward faithful summarization <cite id="30249a55-1">Models can amplify extrinsic hallucinations present in human-written summaries during training</cite> <cite id="30249a55-2">Early correction is crucial; intrinsic/ extrinsic errors propagate in abstractive chains</cite>.
- Combine data selection with model-as-a-metric alignment. Use entailment/QA metrics to generate claim-level feedback and construct preference pairs or policy gradients for RLHF/RLAIF. This provides training signals that directly target hallucination types intrinsic to summarization, reducing errors that extrinsic metrics overlook <cite id="26850444-0">RLHF/RLAIF decompose outputs into atomic claims, assess validity via stronger models, and use scores to train preference policies that reduce hallucinations</cite> <cite id="26850444-4">Open-source AI-feedback alignment reduces object hallucination by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7%, improving both automatic and human evaluations</cite>.
- Monitor and reconcile with human evaluations. Because intrinsic metrics can correlate weakly with human judgments, include periodic human faithfulness assessments and targeted A/B studies. Use multi-metric dashboards (factuality, consistency, relevance, ROUGE) to detect trade-offs and calibrate guardrails for domain-specific tolerance (e.g., clinical inference) <cite id="29b9d831-1">Traditional metrics have poor correlation with human hallucination judgments; FRANK/TRUE provide better alignment and error typing</cite> <cite id="30249a55-4">Domain experts may accept certain inferences not explicitly stated in records, so human context-specific criteria are essential</cite>.

5) Summary
- Training-data interventions prevent hallucinations by shifting supervision from lexical coverage to evidence-backed faithfulness. They do so through data selection/cleaning by factuality metrics, faithfulness-constrained objectives and QA-grounded signals, early error correction to avoid snowballing, and alignment via model-as-a-metric and AI/peer feedback. These methods directly address intrinsic hallucinations that extrinsic metrics miss, often improving human faithfulness and factuality without sacrificing informativeness, and in some cases yielding large absolute reductions in hallucination rates <cite id="30249a55-3">Contrastive parameter ensembling improves factual entailment accuracy by up to 16.69% and 15.78% while preserving ROUGE</cite> <cite id="29b9d831-0">QA-based and entailment metrics better capture factual consistency than ROUGE, explaining their utility in training</cite> <cite id="26850444-4">RLAIF-V reduces object hallucination by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7% with improved human evaluations</cite>. When intrinsic and extrinsic metrics disagree, these interventions provide training signals that operationalize human-like faithfulness, narrowing the gap between automatic proxies and human error judgments <cite id="29b9d831-1">Faithfulness metrics show varied correlations with human judgments, motivating multi-metric, data-centric interventions</cite> <cite id="30249a55-0">Intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations are conflated in many automatic metrics, complicating single-number evaluations</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
Snippet: Existing metrics for hallucination in abstractive summarization are mainly model based. Following Huang et al. [57], we divide the hallucination metrics into two categories: (1) unsupervised metrics and (2) semi-supervised metrics. Existing hallucination metrics evaluate both intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations together because it is difficult to automatically distinguish them.

Title: Improved Beam Search for Hallucination Mitigation in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: summarization (Ji et al., 2022) documented an extensive survey on hallucinations present in various NLP downstream tasks. They discuss the different hallucination mitigation methods with respect to these tasks and summarize the metrics to measure hallucination. An abstract summary is defined to be hallucinated if it has any spans of text not semantically supported by the input document. Hallucinations can be categorized into two major types -intrinsic and extrinsic. Intrinsic hallucinations refer to the contradictions in the abstract summary with respect to the input document: for example, using wrong pronouns, swapping names and verbs. Models like FactCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020) trained on minor text transformations can be used to detect such errors. Extrinsic hallucinations refer to the unsupported spans of text present in the generated summaries that cannot be verified only with the input document. It arises partly due to the extrinsic hallucinations present in human written summaries which the model overfits during training process. (Dziri et al., 2022) studied hallucinations in conversational models using their corresponding datasets and observed that Sequence-2-Sequence models like GPT-2 not only hallucinate but also amplify the percentage of hallucinations with respect to the training data. (Cao et al., 2022;Dong et al., 2022) inspect whether the hallucinations generated in summary align with world knowledge.

Title: Mitigating Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization with Domain-Conditional Mutual Information
Snippet: In abstractive summarization, hallucinations occur when the generated content diverges from the source material, categorized as intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations (Maynez et al., 2020).Intrinsic hallucinations arise from generating content that contradicts the input source document, while extrinsic hallucinations occur from ignoring the source (Ji et al., 2023).Our focus lies in summarization, where a quality summary mirrors the source's content.Thus, reducing hallucinations entails increasing faithfulness and factual consistency between the source document and the generated summary.(Zhang et al., 2023) highlighted the snowball effect of hallucination: initial inaccuracies tend to propagate subsequent incorrect explanations due to initial commitment.Language models, trained on data where the correct answer precedes the explanation, tend to align subsequent explanations with initial inaccuracies.Hence, early correction of hallucinated content is crucial.

Title: CaPE: Contrastive Parameter Ensembling for Reducing Hallucination in Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: Hallucination is a known issue for neural abstractive summarization models. Recent work suggests that the degree of hallucination may depend on errors in the training data. In this work, we propose a new method called Contrastive Parameter Ensembling (CaPE) to use training data more effectively, utilizing variations in noise in training samples to reduce hallucination. We first select clean and noisy subsets from the training data using different automatic factual metrics. Then, we fine-tune a base summarization model, which is trained on all training samples, on the clean (noisy) subset to obtain an \textit{expert} (\textit{anti-expert}) model. Finally, we adjust the parameters of base model by the difference between parameters of the \textit{expert} and \textit{anti-expert} models, steering the base model towards the \textit{expert} model and away from the \textit{anti-expert} model. Experimental results show that CaPE improves performance across different automatic factual metrics and human evaluation, with the maximum improvement of 16.69\% and 15.78\% on summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy for the XSUM and CNN/DM datasets. The improvement in factual performance does not degrade the performance on other metrics of informativeness such as ROUGE.

Title: Is artificial intelligence capable of generating hospital discharge summaries from inpatient records?
Snippet: Some recent studies have attempted to generate a complete discharge summary from the input of free-form inpatient records similar to ours [21][22][23][24][25][26]. While some studies employed extractive methods [23][24][25][26], in other studies, the encoderdecoder architecture of the neural model was used to generate sentences for abstractive summarization [21,22], with a limited number of studies. 

Because abstractive summarization can generate more flexible summaries, it has become a major approach in automatic summarization research [14][15][16][17][18][19]. However, abstractive summarization may sometimes unintentionally generate unfaithful descriptions known as hallucinations. Summaries with hallucinations are fluent [51], but hallucinations degrade the summary quality. Therefore, they have attracted attention in the field [52][53][54][55][56][57]. Maynez et al. (2020) classified hallucinations into two types: intrinsic and extrinsic [51]. Intrinsic hallucination is a phenomenon in which the concept or term itself is in the source documents; its synthesis misrepresents the information in the source, and the meaning becomes inconsistent. Extrinsic hallucination is content that is neither supported nor contradicted by the source and is caused by source documents with poor information. Therefore, the analyses of extrinsic hallucinations in previous studies are almost equal to our investigation of the information sources in discharge summaries. In discharge summaries, complementary statements that are not explicitly stated in inpatient records may be inserted; however, they can be inferred easily by medical professionals. This study does not consider this to be a hallucination if the information can be inferred, although previous studies have defined hallucinations more rigorously. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first attempt to address hallucination problems in the summarization of clinical narratives.

documents.snippet: Hallucination is a known issue for neural abstractive summarization models. Recent work suggests that the degree of hallucination may depend on errors in the training data. In this work, we propose a new method called Contrastive Parameter Ensembling (CaPE) to use training data more effectively, utilizing variations in noise in training samples to reduce hallucination. We first select clean and noisy subsets from the training data using different automatic factual metrics. Then, we fine-tune a base summarization model, which is trained on all training samples, on the clean (noisy) subset to obtain an \textit{expert} (\textit{anti-expert}) model. Finally, we adjust the parameters of base model by the difference between parameters of the \textit{expert} and \textit{anti-expert} models, steering the base model towards the \textit{expert} model and away from the \textit{anti-expert} model. Experimental results show that CaPE improves performance across different automatic factual metrics and human evaluation, with the maximum improvement of 16.69\% and 15.78\% on summary-level dependency-arc entailment accuracy for the XSUM and CNN/DM datasets. The improvement in factual performance does not degrade the performance on other metrics of informativeness such as ROUGE.

documents.title: Is artificial intelligence capable of generating hospital discharge summaries from inpatient records?
documents.snippet:
Some recent studies have attempted to generate a complete discharge summary from the input of free-form inpatient records similar to ours [21][22][23][24][25][26]. While some studies employed extractive methods [23][24][25][26], in other studies, the encoderdecoder architecture of the neural model was used to generate sentences for abstractive summarization [21,22], with a limited number of studies. 

Because abstractive summarization can generate more flexible summaries, it has become a major approach in automatic summarization research [14][15][16][17][18][19]. However, abstractive summarization may sometimes unintentionally generate unfaithful descriptions known as hallucinations. Summaries with hallucinations are fluent [51], but hallucinations degrade the summary quality. Therefore, they have attracted attention in the field [52][53][54][55][56][57]. Maynez et al. (2020) classified hallucinations into two types: intrinsic and extrinsic [51]. Intrinsic hallucination is a phenomenon in which the concept or term itself is in the source documents; its synthesis misrepresents the information in the source, and the meaning becomes inconsistent. Extrinsic hallucination is content that is neither supported nor contradicted by the source and is caused by source documents with poor information. Therefore, the analyses of extrinsic hallucinations in previous studies are almost equal to our investigation of the information sources in discharge summaries. In discharge summaries, complementary statements that are not explicitly stated in inpatient records may be inserted; however, they can be inferred easily by medical professionals. This study does not consider this to be a hallucination if the information can be inferred, although previous studies have defined hallucinations more rigorously. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first attempt to address hallucination problems in the summarization of clinical narratives.

Title: Repairing the Cracked Foundation: A Survey of Obstacles in Evaluation Practices for Generated Text
Snippet: An aspect of quality mentioned above and which permeates all of NLG is faithfulness, and much recent work has focused on this aspect for abstractive summarization. Maynez et al. (2020) state that a model is not faithful if it hallucinates, that is, it adds information that is not present in the source document. They define multiple categories of hallucinations: Intrinsic hallucinations misrepresent facts in the input, for example turning a "former London mayoral candidate" into a "former London mayor". Extrinsic hallucinations ignore the input altogether, for example generating "President Sara" in the example above. Not all hallucinations are problematic-an extrinsic hallucination can be factual, and may, in fact, be desirable depending on the use case. For system evaluation, it is therefore important to be able to discern between hallucinations of different types, which cannot be done by producing a single number. 

Maynez et al. demonstrate that similarity metrics fail to measure faithfulness. The same failure is observed by Pagnoni et al. (2021) who introduce and collect annotations for an alternative typology of factual errors which involves fine-grained categories such as Coreference Error and Out of Article Error. In an alternative approach to measuring correlations with human judgments, Gabriel et al. (2021) inject factual errors in reference summaries, and checks whether system rankings produced by metrics correlate with the "level of factuality" of the transformed sentences, among other properties like a metric's value range and generalization. They also identify that standard evaluation metrics (e.g., ROUGE-L and ROUGE-1) oftentimes fail at capturing factuality, but identify questionanswering metrics as promising, somewhat contradicting Maynez et al.. Similarly, Chen et al. (2021) analyze mispredictions on a set of previously annotated summarization corpora (Kryscinski et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020;Falke et al., 2019;Maynez et al., 2020).

Title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
Snippet: Recently, various studies have illustrated that most conventional metrics used to measure the quality of writing are not adequate for quantifying the level of hallucination [22,26]. It has been shown that State-of-the-Art (SOTA) abstractive summarization systems, evaluated with metrics such as ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR, have hallucinated content in 25% of their generated summaries [32]. A similar phenomenon has been shown in other NLG tasks, where it has been discovered that traditional metrics have a poor correlation with human judgment in terms of the hallucination problem [22,26,54,66]. Therefore, there are active research efforts to define effective metrics for quantifying hallucination, as summarized in Table 2. FRANK [99] surveys the faithfulness metrics for summarization and compares these metrics' correlations with human judgments. To assess the example-level accuracy of metrics in diverse tasks, TRUE [53] reports their area under the ROC curve (ROC AUC) in regard to hallucinated example detection.

Title: BRIDO: Bringing Democratic Order to Abstractive Summarization
Snippet: We choose the metrics to cover the various summarization and hallucination metrics. 

ROUGE Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (Lin 2004) measures the lexical similarity between summaries and human-written references by comparing the overlap of n-grams, which are sequences of n words. The most common variants of ROUGE include ROUGE-N (for n-gram matching) and ROUGE-L (for longest common subsequence matching). Among these, we use ROUGE-1 (R-1), ROUGE-2 (R-2), and ROUGE-L (R-L) for evaluation. For the ranking, we use 2 R-1 × R-2/(R-1 + R-2) for XSum and (R-1 + R-2 + R-L)/3 for CNN/DM following Liu et al. (2022a). ROUGE's limitation includes the lexical bias and the questionable quality of the reference. In this work, we generalize this conventional definition of ROUGE and use it to measure the lexical similarity between summary candidates as well. 

QAFactEval (Fabbri et al. 2022) is a QA-Based Factual Consistency Evaluation without a reference. Given a summary and the source document, it uses a question generation model to generate questions for each of the named entities. It then uses the source document as a reference for the question-answering model to generate the answers for each question. It evaluates the answers with the true answer and measures the consistency of a summary with its source document. The submetrics (LERC, F1, EM, and IsAns) are the methods used in comparing the model answer with the true answer. LERC has a maximum score of 5 and F1, EM, and IsAns are measured in percent. QAFactEval, like all other QA-based factuality metrics, suffers from bias towards extractive summaries. (Liu et al. 2023b) is a framework for using large language models with chain-of-thoughts (CoT) and a formfilling paradigm to assess the quality of NLG outputs. G-Eval consists of four sub-metrics which are coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance.

Title: HaRiM^+: Evaluating Summary Quality with Hallucination Risk
Snippet: Although recent state-of-the-art summarization models have achieved remarkable performances (Lewis et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020), appropriate metrics for measuring faithfulness of the generated summaries are still needed. The practice of measuring performance in the summarization task heavily relies on the N-gram matching based metric, ROUGE (Lin, 2004). Reportedly, ROUGE barely satisfies more than indicating lexical similarity (Maynez et al., 2020) and does not consider semantic dimensions of the generation, which current research needs of. 

There have been numerous attempts to come up with faithfulness evaluation metrics (Novikova et al., 2017;Peyrard, 2019). Neural-based metrics have demonstrated good performances in estimating the factual consistency of a summaryarticle pair with semantic entailment (Kryscinski et al., 2020;Goyal and Durrett, 2020), questionanswering framework (Wang et al., 2020;Scialom et al., 2021Scialom et al., , 2019)), and text generation (Yuan et al., 2021;Xie et al., 2021). Most of the model-asa-metric approach generally requires fine-tuning or complicated pipelines. Consequently, evaluating generated texts with recent model-as-a-metric methods has become cumbersome. 

With the increased demand for faithful generation models, it has come to a lot of attention on reformulating training objectives for purported for this (Zhang et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2022a;Holtzman et al., 2018). We focus on the training objective suggested in (Miao et al., 2021), which directly targets hallucination problems in generating sentences given a source context. Miao et al. suggest that an overconfident decoder causes hallucination since the model excessively pays attention to the previously generated tokens over the source context which is in line with (Bowman et al., 2016).

Title: A Graph-theoretic Summary Evaluation for ROUGE
Snippet: We evaluate ROUGE-G, against the top metrics (C S IIITH3, DemokritosGR1, Catolicasc1) among the 23 metrics participated in TAC AESOP 2011, ROUGE, and the most recent related work (ROUGE-WE) (Table 1). Overall results support our proposal to consider semantics besides surface with ROUGE. Since the large/small differences in competing correlations with human assessment are not an acceptable proof of superiority/inferiority in performance of one metric over another, significance tests should be applied. To better clarify the effectiveness of ROUGE-G, we have used pairwise Williams significance test recommended by Graham et al. (2015) for summarization evaluation. Accordingly, evaluation of a given summarization metric, M new , takes the form of quantifying three correlations: r(M new , H), that exists between the evaluation metric scores for summarization systems and corresponding human assessment scores; r(M base , H), that stands for the correlation of baseline metrics with human judges; and the third correlation, between evaluation metric scores themselves, r(M base , M new ). It can happen for a pair of competing metrics for which the correlation between metric scores is strong, that a small difference in competing correlations with human assessment is significant, while, for a different pair of metrics with a larger difference in correlation, the difference is not significant (Graham et al., 2015). Using this significance test, the results show that all increases in correlations of ROUGE-G compared to ROUGE and ROUGE-WE variants are statistically significant (p < 0.05). We analyze the correlation results reported in Table 1 in the following. ROUGE-G-2 achieves the best correlation with Pyramid, regarding all correlation metrics. Moreover, every ROUGE-G variant outperforms its corresponding ROUGE and ROUGE-WE variants, regardless of the correlation metric used. However, the only exception is ROUGE-SU4, which correlates slightly better with Pyramid when measuring with Pearson correlation. One possible reason is that Pyramid measures content similarity between peer and model summaries, while the variants of ROUGE-G favor semantics behind the content for measuring similarities.

Title: Self-Consistency as a Free Lunch: Reducing Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models via Self-Reflection
Snippet: To address uncertainty and over-reliance on biased patterns in training data, several works focus on detecting hallucinations with external feedback within its outputs. First type of feedback is through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [24] to guide the models respond based on visual-grounded cues. Silkie [33] utilizes the powerful GPT-4V [4] to generate feedback to help it generate visually faithful responses. A recent method RLAIF-V [16] incorporate a divide-and-conquer strategy, where responses are split into atomic claims, allowing models to evaluate the validity of each component. This approach assesses the validity of each claim using either an external powerful VLM or the original model with binary questions. Then the responses are rated using the produced validity scores and used to generate training pairs for Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) [34]. This approach relies on peer feedback-using other opensource MLLMs as the feedback source. While it avoids dependence on powerful external superior models used in superior-teacher methods, it still requires additional models and cannot reduce hallucinations on its own. In contrast to existing work, we focus on harvesting feedback from the target model itself, which does not require expansive human annotation or powerful external models.

Title: Volcano: Mitigating Multimodal Hallucination through Self-Feedback Guided Revision
Snippet: Previous methods for mitigating multimodal hallucinations have varied in their focus, including enhancing the quality of instruction tuning data, model training methodologies, and implementing post-hoc refinements. LRV-Instruction dataset (Liu et al., 2023a) ensures the balance of both negative and positive instructions and VIGC (Wang et al., 2023a) iteratively generates and corrects instructions to reduce hallucinated samples in training data. Adapting reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to train a single reward model as in LLaVA-RLHF (Sun et al., 2023) or training multiple or even without no reward models as in FDPO (Gunjal et al., 2023) has proven effective as well. LURE (Zhou et al., 2023) trains a revision model to detect and correct hallucinated objects in the base model's response. Woodpecker (Yin et al., 2023) breaks down the revision process into multiple subtasks where three pre-trained models apart from the base LMM are employed for the subtasks. 

Unlike models using reinforcement learning, our approach does not require reward model training. Also, contrary to revision-only methods, our method trains a model to self -revise, eliminating the need for extra modules. Furthermore, we introduce natural language feedback before the revision process. This feedback serves a dual purpose: it revisits the visual features for enhanced clarity and specifically pinpoints the hallucinated elements that require correction, thereby enriching the information available for more effective revision.

Snippet: Alignment methods such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) have been shown to reduce hallucinations but not eliminate them. (Ouyang et al., 2022) introduced SFT followed by RLHF using human demonstrations, while (Bai et al., 2022) optimized preference models to balance helpfulness and harmlessness; both approaches rely on costly human feedback and do not explicitly model uncertainty. (Lambert et al., 2025) surveyed these methods, identifying hallucination as a persistent failure mode and motivating the need for more verifiable reward structures. 

More closely related, (Godin et al., 2019) proposed a ternary reward structure that explicitly rewards abstention in question answering, improving precision and reducing hallucinations. However, this work predates modern instruction-tuned LLMs and does not study abstention within contemporary SFT or RL-based training pipelines. In contrast, our work integrates abstention-aware supervision into modern LLM alignment and evaluation, enabling calibrated refusal behavior without relying solely on dense human preference feedback.

Title: RLAIF-V: Open-Source AI Feedback Leads to Super GPT-4V Trustworthiness
Snippet: Traditional feedback learning for hallucination reduction relies on labor-intensive manual labeling or expensive proprietary models. This leaves the community without foundational knowledge about how to build high-quality feedback with open-source MLLMs. In this work, we introduce RLAIF-V, a novel framework that aligns MLLMs in a fully open-source paradigm. RLAIF-V maximally explores open-source MLLMs from two perspectives, including high-quality feedback data generation for preference learning and self-feedback guidance for inference-time scaling. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks in both automatic and human evaluation show that RLAIF-V substantially enhances the trustworthiness of models at both preference learning and inference time. RLAIF-V 7B reduces object hallucination by 80.7% and overall hallucination by 33.7%. Remarkably, RLAIF-V 12B further reveals the self-alignment potential of open-source MLLMs, where the model can learn from feedback of itself to achieve super GPT-4V trustworthiness.

snippet.text: To address uncertainty and over-reliance on biased patterns in training data, several works focus on detecting hallucinations with external feedback within its outputs. First type of feedback is through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [24] to guide the models respond based on visual-grounded cues. Silkie [33] utilizes the powerful GPT-4V [4] to generate feedback to help it generate visually faithful responses. A recent method RLAIF-V [16] incorporate a divide-and-conquer strategy, where responses are split into atomic claims, allowing models to evaluate the validity of each component. This approach assesses the validity of each claim using either an external powerful VLM or the original model with binary questions. Then the responses are rated using the produced validity scores and used to generate training pairs for Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) [34]. This approach relies on peer feedback-using other opensource MLLMs as the feedback source. While it avoids dependence on powerful external superior models used in superior-teacher methods, it still requires additional models and cannot reduce hallucinations on its own. In contrast to existing work, we focus on harvesting feedback from the target model itself, which does not require expansive human annotation or powerful external models.
